evidence.snippet: two siblings, born to consanguineous parents, who presented with encephalopathy, developmental regression, hypotonia
evidence.explanation: Encephalopathy is documented in the COX4I1 siblings with the Leigh-like presentation.

steps/7.description: Encephalopathy, a core feature of the severe (P152T) sibling presentation.

steps/8.description: Elevated blood and CSF lactate from the bioenergetic block in cytochrome c oxidase, the clinical manifestation of the "Lactic Acidosis and Metabolic Decompensation" pathophysiology node and a defining biochemical feature of the Leigh-syndrome-spectrum presentation of COX4I1 deficiency.

edges/1.description: Loss of the COX4-1 subunit yields a catalytically deficient holoenzyme.

edges/2.description: A dysfunctional Complex IV leaks reactive oxygen species, driving oxidative stress and genomic instability.

edges/3.description: Loss of oxidative ATP synthesis forces anaerobic glycolysis and lactate accumulation.

edges/4.description: The bioenergetic deficit is most damaging in high oxidative-demand tissues, notably the brain.

edges/5.description: Oxidative stress is associated with increased chromosomal breaks that simulate Fanconi anemia.

edges/6.description: Lactate overproduction manifests clinically as lactic acidosis.

edges/7.description: Bioenergetic failure in the brain produces encephalopathy and developmental regression.

evidence.snippet: Whole Exome Sequencing was performed then followed by Sanger confirmation, identified a K101N mutation in COX4I1, segregating with the disease.
evidence.explanation: Identifies a homozygous K101N COX4I1 variant segregating with disease, establishing COX4I1 as the causal gene.

evidence.snippet: Our results demonstrate the first human mutation in the COX4I1 gene linked to diseases and confirm its role in the pathogenesis.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the first human COX4I1 disease association and confirms its causal role.

evidence.snippet: Review management of nuclear gene-encoded LSS with a focus on disorders with targeted therapies
evidence.explanation: The GeneReviews overview frames management of the nuclear gene-encoded Leigh syndrome spectrum, the clinical context for supportive care.

treatments/0.description: There is no disease-modifying therapy for COX4I1-related COX deficiency. Management of the nuclear gene-encoded Leigh syndrome spectrum is largely supportive, with surveillance and symptomatic treatment of seizures, feeding difficulties, and metabolic decompensation.

evidence.snippet: The encoded protein, complexin 1, is crucially involved in neuronal synaptic regulation, and homozygous Cplx1 knockout mice have the earliest known onset of ataxia seen in a mouse model.
evidence.explanation: Identifies complexin-1 as a synaptic regulator whose loss causes neurological disease, the trigger of this node.

evidence.snippet: loss of complexin 1 function may lead to a complex but variable clinical phenotype
evidence.explanation: Frames the disorder as a loss-of-complexin-1-function condition.

steps/0.description: Biallelic loss-of-function variants in CPLX1 abolish complexin-1, a cytosolic protein crucially involved in neuronal synaptic regulation. Complexin-1 binds the assembled SNARE complex, acting as a fusion clamp and a facilitator of calcium-triggered release, so its loss removes a key regulator of the fusion machinery.

evidence.snippet: Neuronal SNAREs and their key regulators together drive synaptic vesicle exocytosis and synaptic transmission as a single integrated membrane fusion machine.
evidence.explanation: Establishes complexin-1 (a key SNARE regulator) as part of the integrated fusion machine impaired in this disorder.

evidence.snippet: The encoded protein, complexin 1, is crucially involved in neuronal synaptic regulation
evidence.explanation: Links complexin-1's synaptic-regulatory (fusion-clamp) role to the disorder.

steps/1.description: Complexin-1 is a key regulator of the SNARE fusion machine: it clamps the assembled SNARE complex to prevent premature vesicle fusion and, together with synaptotagmin-1, synchronizes calcium-triggered release. Loss of complexin-1 dysregulates calcium-triggered SNARE-mediated fusion, degrading the temporal control of neurotransmitter release. This is the module's key conformance target — the fusion-machinery arm, here at the level of the SNARE-complex regulator rather than a SNARE subunit.

evidence.snippet: All displayed marked developmental delay and migrating myoclonic epilepsy, and one showed a cerebellar cleft in addition.
evidence.explanation: Documents the severe epilepsy (migrating myoclonic seizures) and developmental impairment produced by the disorder.

steps/2.description: Dysregulated, poorly synchronized neurotransmitter release disturbs cortical excitatory/inhibitory balance, producing neuronal hyperexcitability and a severe infantile epilepsy (migrating myoclonic seizures), together with impaired activity-dependent neurodevelopment.

evidence.snippet: All displayed marked developmental delay and migrating myoclonic epilepsy, and one showed a cerebellar cleft in addition.
evidence.explanation: Documents migrating myoclonic epilepsy as a core feature.

steps/3.description: Severe infantile epilepsy with migrating myoclonic seizures.

evidence.snippet: All displayed marked developmental delay and migrating myoclonic epilepsy
evidence.explanation: Documents marked developmental delay as a universal feature.

steps/4.description: Marked developmental delay in all affected individuals.

evidence.snippet: complexin simultaneously suppressed spontaneous fusion and activated fast calcium ion-evoked fusion
evidence.explanation: Complexin acts directly on the SNARE fusion machine, so its loss deregulates SNARE-mediated fusion — the mechanism of this edge.

evidence.snippet: identified homozygous CPLX1 variants in three patients with ID from two unrelated families. All displayed marked developmental delay and migrating myoclonic epilepsy
evidence.explanation: Biallelic loss of complexin-1 co-segregates with migrating myoclonic epilepsy in three patients from two unrelated families, which is the genotype-to-seizure association this edge asserts. It establishes the endpoint rather than demonstrating the intervening excitability change; the relative contribution of the clamp and facilitator arms is recorded as an open question in the discussions section.

evidence.snippet: All displayed marked developmental delay and migrating myoclonic epilepsy, and one showed a cerebellar cleft in addition.
evidence.explanation: Every reported CPLX1-null individual had migrating myoclonic epilepsy, the clinical seizure phenotype this edge produces.

evidence.snippet: All displayed marked developmental delay and migrating myoclonic epilepsy, and one showed a cerebellar cleft in addition.
evidence.explanation: Marked developmental delay co-occurred with the epilepsy in all reported individuals, supporting this edge to the developmental phenotype.

evidence.snippet: Recently, a homozygous truncating variant in CPLX1 was suggested to be causative for migrating epilepsy and structural brain abnormalities.
evidence.explanation: Corroborates biallelic loss-of-function CPLX1 as causative of migrating epilepsy with brain abnormalities.

genes/0.notes: Biallelic (homozygous) loss-of-function CPLX1 variants, including truncating variants, cause the disorder; a homozygous truncating variant was also independently linked to migrating epilepsy and structural brain abnormalities.

evidence.snippet: We identified a homozygous nonsense mutation (NM_006651:c.G322T:p.E108X) in the CPLX1 gene in two female siblings, BAB6167 and BAB6168, who presented with malignant migrating epilepsy and cortical atrophy.
evidence.explanation: Establishes malignant migrating epilepsy as the seizure syndrome this treatment targets. The paper reports no treatment or response, so the choice of antiseizure medication follows from the syndrome rather than from CPLX1-specific evidence.

treatments/0.description: Seizures are managed with antiseizure medications; the severe migrating myoclonic epilepsy is often refractory. Treatment here is inferred from the seizure syndrome rather than from CPLX1-specific data - the published CPLX1 reports characterize the epilepsy but do not report which agents were tried or how patients responded.

evidence.snippet: All displayed marked developmental delay and migrating myoclonic epilepsy, and one showed a cerebellar cleft in addition.
evidence.explanation: Marked developmental delay was present in every reported patient, which is what the developmental therapies in this treatment are directed at.

treatments/1.description: Multidisciplinary supportive care with developmental therapies is the mainstay.

evidence.snippet: we performed trio-based WES in 311 patients with unsolved ID and additional clinical features, and identified homozygous CPLX1 variants in three patients with ID from two unrelated families
evidence.explanation: Homozygous variants in unrelated families are the basis for counseling autosomal-recessive inheritance and its 25% sibling recurrence risk.

evidence.snippet: We identified a homozygous nonsense mutation (NM_006651:c.G322T:p.E108X) in the CPLX1 gene in two female siblings, BAB6167 and BAB6168, who presented with malignant migrating epilepsy and cortical atrophy.
evidence.explanation: An affected sibling pair homozygous for the same nonsense allele is the recurrence event counseling has to convey to families.

treatments/2.description: Genetic counseling addresses the autosomal-recessive inheritance and 25% sibling recurrence risk.

evidence.snippet: complexin simultaneously suppressed spontaneous fusion and activated fast calcium ion-evoked fusion
evidence.explanation: Establishes complexin's dual clamp (suppresses spontaneous) and facilitator (activates evoked) function, the two arms whose relative contribution to CPLX1 disease is the open question.

evidence.snippet: Neuronal SNAREs and their key regulators together drive synaptic vesicle exocytosis and synaptic transmission as a single integrated membrane fusion machine.
evidence.explanation: Frames complexin-1 as a key SNARE regulator within the fusion machine, whose specific loss-of-function mode is unresolved.

open_questions/0.rationale: Complexin's dual clamp/facilitator function means CPLX1 loss can degrade synaptic transmission by two mechanistically opposite routes: unclamping spontaneous (calcium-independent) fusion, and abolishing the synchronized calcium-triggered evoked release. These have different predicted circuit consequences (tonic noise versus loss of phasic drive), so which predominates in human CPLX1-null neurons is unresolved and bears directly on how the "dysregulated fusion" node should be interpreted and, ultimately, on rational therapy.

evidence.snippet: loss of complexin 1 function may lead to a complex but variable clinical phenotype
evidence.explanation: The reporting authors explicitly flag phenotypic variability, motivating the phenotype-definition gap.

evidence.snippet: All displayed marked developmental delay and migrating myoclonic epilepsy, and one showed a cerebellar cleft in addition.
evidence.explanation: Documents the mixed epileptic, developmental, and structural/cerebellar features underlying the lump/split question.

open_questions/1.rationale: Reported CPLX1-null individuals show a complex and variable phenotype spanning severe infantile epileptic encephalopathy, developmental impairment, structural brain changes, and (in the mouse) prominent ataxia/movement features. Whether the human disorder is fundamentally an epileptic encephalopathy, a neurodegenerative/movement disorder, or a unified spectrum is a genuine phenotype-definition (lump/split) gap that is currently unresolvable from the small published cohort and affects how this entry's boundaries and downstream nodes should be drawn.

evidence.snippet: homozygous Cplx1 knockout mice have the earliest known onset of ataxia seen in a mouse model.
evidence.explanation: Shows the mouse phenotype is dominated by early ataxia, not the cortical epilepsy that defines the human disorder — the basis of the mismatch.

open_questions/2.rationale: The principal in vivo evidence for CPLX1 loss is the Cplx1-knockout mouse, whose most striking, earliest phenotype is ataxia (a cerebellar/motor feature) rather than the severe cortical epileptic encephalopathy that defines the human disorder. This is a translational-fidelity mismatch: the model clearly demonstrates that complexin-1 loss is neurologically catastrophic, but whether it reproduces the human seizure/cortical phenotype — as opposed to a predominantly movement phenotype — is the open question, so its evidence weight for the seizure node should be qualified.

evidence.snippet: In all the families, we identified a heterozygous variant in SGMS2, a gene prominently expressed in cortical bone and encoding the plasma membrane-resident sphingomyelin synthase SMS2.
evidence.explanation: The discovery finding, establishing the gene, its heterozygous dominant action, its bone expression, and the normal plasma-membrane residence of its product.

evidence.snippet: Four unrelated families shared the same nonsense variant, c.148C>T (p.Arg50*), whereas the other families had a missense variant, c.185T>G (p.Ile62Ser) or c.191T>G (p.Met64Arg).
evidence.explanation: Names the three founding alleles and the two allele classes the mechanism turns on.

steps/1.description: The primary lesion is a heterozygous variant in SGMS2 on chromosome 4, encoding sphingomyelin synthase 2. The published allelic series was for years only three variants - the recurrent nonsense c.148C>T (p.Arg50*) and two missense alleles at adjacent residues, c.185T>G (p.Ile62Ser) and c.191T>G (p.Met64Arg) - which is a remarkably tight series for a dominant skeletal disease and is what made the allele-class comparison below possible. A frameshift allele with a high-bone-mass presentation has since been reported. SGMS2 is prominently expressed in cortical bone.

evidence.snippet: While the p.Arg50* mutation yielded a catalytically inactive enzyme, p.Ile62Ser and p.Met64Arg each enhanced the rate of de novo sphingomyelin production by blocking export of a functional enzyme from the endoplasmic reticulum.
evidence.explanation: The functional experiment establishing the two allele classes and, crucially, that the severe alleles increase rather than decrease sphingomyelin synthesis.

evidence.snippet: The missense variants uphold SMS2 in the ER, while the p.Arg50* variant dislocates SMS2 into the cis/medial-Golgi.
evidence.explanation: States the specific mislocalisation destination for each allele class, which is what makes mislocalisation rather than activity the shared lesion.

evidence.snippet: However, SGMS2 variants affect the cellular localization of SMS2 resulting in misdirected SM synthesis and disruption of plasma membrane SM asymmetry.
evidence.explanation: Names the two proximate consequences - misdirected synthesis and loss of plasma-membrane asymmetry - that this node asserts.

evidence.snippet: we show that SMS2 variants linked to the most severe bone phenotypes retain full enzymatic activity but fail to leave the ER owing to a defective autonomous ER export signal
evidence.explanation: The dedicated mechanistic study, and the primary source for this node's central claim: the severe alleles are fully active and the lesion is a defective ER export signal, not a loss of catalysis.

evidence.snippet: Cells harboring pathogenic SMS2 variants accumulate sphingomyelin in the ER and display a disrupted transbilayer sphingomyelin asymmetry.
evidence.explanation: Demonstrates the two lipid consequences - ectopic ER sphingomyelin and loss of transbilayer asymmetry - that follow from the export failure.

steps/2.description: The convergence point, and the reason two biochemically opposite allele classes cause one disease. Normal SMS2 is made in the ER and trafficked to the plasma membrane, where it synthesises sphingomyelin and maintains membrane lipid asymmetry. The missense alleles hold a catalytically competent SMS2 in the ER by blocking its export; the p.Arg50* product is reported to be dislocated into the cis/medial-Golgi. In both cases sphingomyelin synthesis is misdirected away from the plasma membrane. The striking corollary is that the missense alleles INCREASE total de novo sphingomyelin production while causing the more severe disease, which rules out a simple sphingomyelin-deficiency model.

evidence.snippet: These aberrant sphingomyelin distributions also occur in patient-derived fibroblasts and are accompanied by imbalances in cholesterol organization, glycerophospholipid profiles, and lipid order in the secretory pathway.
evidence.explanation: Establishes that the lipid disturbance extends beyond sphingomyelin and is present in patient material, not only in engineered cell systems.

evidence.snippet: We postulate that pathogenic SMS2 variants undermine the capacity of osteogenic cells to uphold nonrandom lipid distributions that are critical for their bone forming activity.
evidence.explanation: Graded PARTIAL and quoted for its hedge. The authors postulate the link to bone-forming activity rather than demonstrate it, and this entry does not upgrade their claim.

steps/3.description: The step that converts a mislocalised enzyme into a cell-biological defect. Sphingomyelin made in the trans-Golgi normally traps ER-synthesised cholesterol and builds a sphingomyelin/sterol gradient along the secretory pathway - a gradient that marks the physical transition in membrane properties defining organelle identity. Pathogenic SMS2 makes sphingomyelin in the ER instead, and the consequence is not confined to sphingomyelin: cholesterol organisation, glycerophospholipid profiles and membrane lipid order are all disturbed, in patient-derived fibroblasts as well as in engineered cells. The authors' proposal is that osteogenic cells cannot sustain the non-random lipid distributions their bone-forming activity requires.

evidence.snippet: Last, osteocyte lacunae appeared abnormally large and round in shape and the canalicular network severely disturbed with short-spanned canaliculi lacking any orderliness or continuity.
evidence.explanation: The direct microscopic observation of the lacunocanalicular defect.

evidence.snippet: Taken together, these data underline a central role for functional SMS2 in bone matrix organization and mineralization, lacunocanalicular network, and in maintaining skeletal strength and integrity.
evidence.explanation: The authors' own synthesis linking SMS2 function to the three tissue-level defects this entry models.

steps/4.description: A second, independent tissue lesion. Osteocyte lacunae are abnormally large and round, and the canalicular network is severely disturbed, with short canaliculi lacking orderliness or continuity. This matters because the lacunocanalicular network is how bone senses mechanical load and coordinates remodelling; a plasma-membrane lipid defect impairing the formation of these fine cell processes is a mechanistically coherent - though not directly demonstrated - explanation.

evidence.snippet: Osteoclast formation and function in vitro was normal.
evidence.explanation: The negative result excluding an osteoclast-driven mechanism.

evidence.snippet: Although these findings suggest increased osteoclast numbers, functional analysis found no differences in osteoclast morphology or resorptive capacity.
evidence.explanation: States explicitly that the histological appearance suggests increased osteoclasts but function is normal, which is why this node exists.

steps/5.description: A deliberate negative node. Bone volume is reduced and the histology could superficially suggest increased resorption, but osteoclast formation and function in vitro were normal, and functional analysis found no difference in osteoclast morphology or resorptive capacity. This is what excludes the high-resorption model that would otherwise be the default reading of an osteoporosis phenotype - and it has a direct therapeutic implication, since antiresorptives are the standard osteoporosis drugs.

evidence.snippet: Bone biopsies showed markedly altered bone material characteristics, including defective bone mineralization.
evidence.explanation: The discovery cohort's biopsy finding of a bone material and mineralization defect.

evidence.snippet: qBEI showed low and heterogeneous matrix mineralization (CaPeak -2.41 SD, -3.72 SD; CaWidth +7.47 SD, +4.41 SD) with a chaotic arrangement of collagenous fibrils under polarized light.
evidence.explanation: Quantifies the mineral defect and the collagen disorganisation by qBEI and polarised light microscopy.

evidence.snippet: Bone histomorphometry portrayed largely normal values for structural and turnover parameters, but in both patient 1 and patient 2, respectively, osteoid thickness (-1.80 SD, -1.37 SD) and mineralizing surface (-1.03 SD, -2.73 SD) were reduced and osteoid surface increased (+9.03 SD, +0.98 SD), leading to elevated mineralization lag time (+8.16 SD, +4.10 SD).
evidence.explanation: The histomorphometric result showing normal turnover with a specifically prolonged mineralization lag time - the finding that makes this a material rather than a remodelling defect.

steps/6.description: The core skeletal lesion, and it is a MATERIAL defect rather than a turnover defect. Transiliac biopsies from two adult p.Arg50* carriers showed largely normal structural and turnover histomorphometry, but reduced osteoid thickness and mineralizing surface with increased osteoid surface - giving a greatly prolonged mineralization lag time - and low, heterogeneous matrix mineral on quantitative backscattered electron imaging, with collagen fibrils chaotically arranged under polarised light. Bone is being made at a normal rate and then mineralised badly.

evidence.snippet: The cranial sclerotic, circular lesions differentiate this skeletal disorder from other types of primary osteoporosis.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the cranial lesions as the discriminating feature of the entity.

evidence.snippet: Calvarial Doughnut Lesions with Bone Fragility (CDL) is an autosomal dominant genetic disease, characterized by low bone mineral density, multiple fractures starting in childhood, and sclerotic doughnut-shaped lesions in the cranial bones.
evidence.explanation: States the coexistence of generalised low BMD with focal cranial sclerosis that this node records as unexplained.

steps/7.description: The pathognomonic finding and the entry's most conspicuous unexplained feature: discrete ring-shaped sclerotic lesions in the cranial bones, coexisting with generalised low bone mineral density elsewhere. A disease that under-mineralises the skeleton produces focal HYPER-sclerosis in the calvaria, and no mechanism has been proposed for that inversion. The lesions are what distinguish CDL from other primary osteoporoses, including osteogenesis imperfecta.

evidence.snippet: The disease manifests as early-onset osteoporosis or a more severe skeletal dysplasia with low bone mineral density, frequent fractures, long-bone deformities, and multiple sclerotic cranial lesions.
evidence.explanation: States the clinical fragility phenotype and its severity range.

steps/8.description: The clinical endpoint: low bone mineral density with recurrent low-trauma spinal and peripheral fractures from childhood, ranging from vertebral compression fractures to dozens of long-bone fractures over a lifetime. The fracture burden can be extreme - one proband had sustained about 40 fractures by age 29.

evidence.snippet: Several subjects had experienced peripheral facial nerve palsy or other neurological manifestations.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the cranial neuropathy as part of the phenotype in the discovery cohort.

evidence.snippet: These findings suggest that SGMS2 variants modulate circadian rhythm and gap junction assembly, adversely affecting bone health and homeostasis, and may affect neuron-supporting cells in SGMS2-related osteoporosis.
evidence.explanation: Graded PARTIAL and cited for the hedge it contains - the authors say "may affect", from fibroblast transcriptomics rather than nerve tissue, so it supports a neural arm as a hypothesis and not as a demonstrated mechanism.

evidence.snippet: several patients experience neurological symptoms, the most frequent being transitory, spontaneously resolving, and recurrent cranial nerve palsies
evidence.explanation: Characterises the palsies as transient, self-resolving and recurrent - the temporal profile this entry argues fits a conduction or lipid mechanism better than progressive foraminal compression.

steps/9.description: Recurrent transient peripheral facial nerve palsy is the commonest, together with trochlear, oculomotor and abducens palsies, transient diplopia and ptosis in individual patients. Two candidate explanations exist and have not been separated: mechanical compression of nerves in sclerotic cranial foramina, or a primary effect of disordered sphingomyelin metabolism on nerve or myelin - sphingomyelin being a major myelin lipid. A transcriptomic study found the differentially expressed genes enriched for neurological as well as skeletal processes and suggested an effect on neuron-supporting cells, which favours but does not establish the second.

edges/2.description: Both allele classes displace SMS2 from its normal plasma-membrane site of action, by different routes.

edges/3.description: Sphingomyelin made in the wrong compartment perturbs the sphingomyelin/sterol gradient that organises the whole secretory pathway.

edges/4.description: Loss of plasma-membrane sphingomyelin impairs mineralization. The steps between the membrane lipid defect and the mineral defect are not established.

edges/5.description: How a disturbed membrane lipid landscape translates into a prolonged mineralization lag time is not established.

edges/6.description: Canaliculi are thin cytoplasmic processes whose formation and maintenance depend on plasma-membrane composition, so a disturbed membrane lipid landscape is the natural upstream candidate for the disrupted network. The edge is INDIRECT_UNKNOWN_INTERMEDIATES because nothing establishes the steps between them - this is a coherence argument about what membranes are needed for, not a measured pathway.

edges/7.description: Poorly and heterogeneously mineralised matrix with disordered collagen is mechanically weak.

edges/8.description: A disordered osteocyte network degrades bone quality independently of matrix mineral content.

evidence.snippet: Four unrelated families shared the same nonsense variant, c.148C>T (p.Arg50*), whereas the other families had a missense variant, c.185T>G (p.Ile62Ser) or c.191T>G (p.Met64Arg).
evidence.explanation: Names the three founding alleles recorded in this block.

evidence.snippet: It has thereafter been reported that about two additional families had this variant, confirming it to be the "hot spot" in the SGMS2 gene
evidence.explanation: Establishes c.148C>T as a recurrent hot spot rather than a private family allele.

evidence.snippet: He was found to have a heterozygous frameshift variant c.1052_1074dup in the SGMS2 gene.
evidence.explanation: Adds a fourth allele class. Graded PARTIAL because it is a single case report and its high-bone-mass phenotype is the opposite of the established low-BMD presentation, so it broadens the series without being established.

genes/0.notes:
SGMS2 on chromosome 4 encodes sphingomyelin synthase 2. Inheritance is autosomal dominant through heterozygous variants. Three founding alleles dominate the literature: the recurrent nonsense c.148C>T (p.Arg50*), which is a hot spot found across most reported families and produces a catalytically inactive enzyme, and the missense c.185T>G (p.Ile62Ser) and c.191T>G (p.Met64Arg), which produce active enzyme trapped in the ER. A frameshift allele c.1052_1074dup has since been reported with a high-bone-mass presentation.
Functional impact does not reduce to a single category, which is why it is described here rather than asserted in a slot: p.Arg50* is loss of function, while the missense alleles are better described as mislocalising - they retain and even increase catalytic output while acting dominantly and causing the more severe disease.

evidence.snippet: Bisphosphonate treatment resulted in notable improvement in back pain and quality of life.
evidence.explanation: Reports symptomatic benefit in one family of the discovery cohort. Graded PARTIAL because it is uncontrolled clinical observation in a single patient within a case series, reporting symptoms rather than fracture rate.

evidence.snippet: Bisphosphonate treatment was commenced at 2.6 years because of a radius fracture, lower limb bowing, and platyspondyly and discontinued at age 6 years; no new fractures have occurred thereafter.
evidence.explanation: A fracture-free interval after treatment in one child. Graded PARTIAL - an uncontrolled single-patient observation, and fracture rates in this disease fall with age anyway, so the comparison is confounded.

evidence.snippet: Since the age of 20 years, she received multiple types osteoporosis treatment including; Teriparatide (Forteo), Denosumab (Prolia) and Risedronate (Actonel).
evidence.explanation: Records risedronate among the agents given to one patient, which is why it sits in this entry rather than with the anabolic agent - it is a bisphosphonate and shares their mechanism. Exposure only, no outcome.

treatments/0.description: Bisphosphonates are the treatment actually used - pamidronate and alendronate in the French-Canadian proband from childhood, pamidronate courses in several of the discovery families and in the Belarusian kindred, with reported improvement in back pain, quality of life, bone mineral density, and in some patients cessation of further long-bone fractures. There is a mechanistic tension worth stating: bisphosphonates are ANTIRESORPTIVE, and osteoclast function in this disease was measured and found normal. So the drug is not correcting the demonstrated lesion, which is defective matrix mineralization on a normal-turnover background. The reported benefits are real but come from uncontrolled clinical observation in small families, not from a trial.

treatments/0/targets/0.description: Treatment is directed at the fracture endpoint rather than at the mineralization defect that produces it.

evidence.snippet: Since the age of 20 years, she received multiple types osteoporosis treatment including; Teriparatide (Forteo), Denosumab (Prolia) and Risedronate (Actonel).
evidence.explanation: Records teriparatide exposure in one patient. Graded PARTIAL - the sentence reports what was given with no outcome measure attached, so it establishes use and nothing about efficacy.

treatments/1.description: The mechanistically interesting option, and the one this entry's therapeutic argument turns on. Teriparatide is an ANABOLIC agent that stimulates bone formation, not an antiresorptive. Since the demonstrated lesion here is defective matrix mineralization on a normal-turnover background with measured-normal osteoclast function, an agent that drives formation is better matched to the mechanism than one that suppresses resorption. No outcome is reported for it in CDL. The patient documented as receiving it had already sustained about 40 fractures by then, so this records what was tried, not what worked.

treatments/1/targets/0.description: Teriparatide targets bone FORMATION, which is the arm this disease impairs - in contrast to the antiresorptives, which target an arm measured to be normal. This link is asserted for teriparatide alone and deliberately not for the antiresorptive entries.

evidence.snippet: Since the age of 20 years, she received multiple types osteoporosis treatment including; Teriparatide (Forteo), Denosumab (Prolia) and Risedronate (Actonel).
evidence.explanation: Records denosumab exposure in the same patient. PARTIAL for the same reason - exposure without an outcome measure.

treatments/2.description: A RANKL-targeting monoclonal antibody, and an antiresorptive. It is recorded because it was given, not because the mechanism recommends it: like the bisphosphonates it acts on osteoclast-mediated resorption, which was measured and found normal in this disease. No outcome is reported. It carries no `target_mechanisms` link for exactly that reason - drawing one to the mineralization node would assert the anabolic rationale that belongs to teriparatide.

evidence.snippet: She was prescribed vitamin D supplementation and started Pamidronate treatment (Aredia) until the age of 14 years, when she was switched to Alendronate (Fosamax) for 4–5 months.
evidence.explanation: Records vitamin D given alongside bisphosphonates. PARTIAL - one patient, no separable outcome for the vitamin D arm.

treatments/3.description: Vitamin D supplementation alongside bisphosphonate therapy, and low 25-hydroxyvitamin D has been documented in a reported patient. This is adjunctive and standard-of-care for any osteoporosis rather than disease-specific - it corrects a coexisting deficiency, it does not address the sphingomyelin lesion.

evidence.snippet: She underwent femoral osteotomy at 2.5 years and intramedullary rodding at 15 years but continued to have multiple fractures.
evidence.explanation: Records both procedures and, in the same sentence, that fractures continued - which is why the description presents surgery as mechanical management rather than disease modification.

treatments/4.description: Corrective and stabilising surgery for long-bone deformity and recurrent fracture - femoral osteotomy and intramedullary rodding are both reported. Notably the patient who had both continued to fracture afterwards, which is consistent with surgery addressing deformity and mechanical support rather than the underlying bone material defect.

treatments/4/targets/0.description: Mechanical correction and stabilisation of deformed or repeatedly fractured long bones, without altering matrix mineralization.

open_questions/0.rationale: The doughnut lesions are the pathognomonic feature and the reason the entity was recognised in 1969, yet no mechanism connects them to the demonstrated mineralization defect - they point the opposite way. Candidate explanations (a site-specific difference between intramembranous calvarial and endochondral long-bone ossification, a reactive response to microdamage, a local difference in membrane lipid requirement) have not been tested. The node is deliberately left without an incoming causal edge from the mineralization branch, because drawing one would assert a mechanism nobody has proposed.

open_questions/1.rationale: This inverts the usual dose-response intuition and is the single most informative fact in the entry. The proposed reading - that ER-retained active SMS2 does harm beyond what simply losing the enzyme does, whether by consuming ceramide in the wrong compartment, generating diacylglycerol where it should not be, or acting as a dominant-negative on trafficking - has not been distinguished experimentally. Distinguishing them matters therapeutically: a substrate or enzyme-replacement strategy would help one model and worsen the other.

open_questions/2.rationale: Both are plausible and they predict different management. Compression would make the palsies a mechanical consequence of the calvarial lesions and potentially surgically addressable; a primary lipid effect on neuron-supporting cells would make them an independent arm of the disease. The transient, recurrent, fully recovering character of the palsies fits a lipid or conduction mechanism better than progressive compression, and one patient with palsies had no reported cranial sclerosis - but no study has imaged the foramina during an episode.

open_questions/3.rationale: Osteoclast formation, morphology and resorptive capacity were all measured and found normal, and histomorphometry showed normal turnover. Bisphosphonates nonetheless are what patients receive, by analogy with osteoporosis generally, and uncontrolled reports describe benefit. Whether that benefit reflects a real effect on this mechanism, a nonspecific density gain, or the natural fall in fracture rate with age is untested. A bisphosphonate that further slows mineralization is at least mechanistically conceivable in a disease whose lesion is a prolonged mineralization lag time. The comparison that would answer this is already partly available and has never been made: reported patients have also received TERIPARATIDE, an anabolic agent that drives bone formation rather than suppressing resorption, and formation is the arm this disease actually impairs. No outcome is reported for it, and the one patient documented as receiving it had already sustained about 40 fractures by then - but an anabolic-versus-antiresorptive comparison in SGMS2 disease is the obvious next question, and the mechanism predicts which way it should go.

open_questions/4.rationale: Sms2-deficient mice have no apparent bone abnormality; the murine bone-formation deficit requires additional osteoblast-specific Sms1 deletion, so SMS1 appears to be the limiting isoform in mouse osteoblasts while SGMS2 is the disease gene in humans. This is the reason CDL has no mouse model and drove the move to zebrafish. There is a second reading that is at least as likely and is more useful: since the SEVERE human alleles retain full enzymatic activity and act by ER retention, they may be dominant and gain-of-mislocalisation rather than loss of function - in which case a mouse null models the wrong lesion entirely, and the informative experiment is a knock-in of p.Ile62Ser or p.Met64Arg, which has not been reported.

open_questions/5.rationale: The lacunocanalicular finding comes from transiliac biopsies of two adult males, both carrying p.Arg50*. Since the two allele classes mislocalise SMS2 to different compartments and produce clinically opposite severities, it cannot be assumed the tissue lesion is the same in both. No biopsy data from a missense carrier has been published.

evidence.snippet: Family-based genetic analysis of GME individuals with cardiomyopathic disease identified an Iranian patient with dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM) as a carrier of a novel, homozygous single nucleotide insertion in JPH2 resulting in a stop codon (JPH2-p.E641*).
evidence.explanation: The recessive allele and its consequence, named precisely. The same paper notes that loss-of-function JPH2 variants had not previously been described in disease, only missense ones.

steps/1.description: Biallelic loss-of-function JPH2 alleles remove junctophilin-2. The reported recessive alleles are truncating: a homozygous single-nucleotide insertion producing p.E641* in consanguineous Iranian families, and a nonsense allele in a Finnish childhood cardiomyopathy kindred. This is the axis that separates CMD2E from the dominant JPH2 disease, which runs on missense alleles that alter the protein's regulation of the ryanodine receptor rather than removing it.

evidence.snippet: JPH2 deficiency resulted in loss of excitation-contraction coupling gain, precipitated by a reduction in the number of junctional membrane complexes and increased variability in the plasmalemma-sarcoplasmic reticulum distance.
evidence.explanation: The geometric lesion measured directly: fewer complexes and a more variable membrane separation, with the functional consequence named in the same sentence.

evidence.snippet: Junctophilin-2 (JPH2) is the primary structural protein for the coupling of transverse (T)-tubule associated cardiac L-type Ca channels and type-2 ryanodine receptors on the sarcoplasmic reticulum within junctional membrane complexes (JMCs) in cardiomyocytes.
evidence.explanation: States the protein's structural role and what it couples. It is the introduction to a gene-therapy study rather than that study's finding, which is why it is marked as background.

steps/2.description: Without junctophilin-2 the t-tubule sarcolemma and the junctional sarcoplasmic reticulum are not held together, so the dyad does not assemble and the distance between the two membranes becomes variable. The lesion is geometric: nothing about either channel is altered, they are simply no longer reliably apposed.

evidence.snippet: Excitation-contraction coupling in striated muscle requires proper communication of plasmalemmal voltage-activated Ca2+ channels and Ca2+ release channels on sarcoplasmic reticulum within junctional membrane complexes.
evidence.explanation: The requirement this node's failure violates. It is the paper's background statement of the physiology rather than its result.

evidence.snippet: Cardiac myocytes from the mutant mice showed deficiency of the junctional membrane complexes and abnormal Ca2+ transients.
evidence.explanation: The calcium handling defect measured in null cardiomyocytes, alongside the structural defect that causes it.

steps/3.description: With the dyad disassembled, calcium entering through the L-type channel no longer reliably reaches a ryanodine receptor, so the amplification step of excitation-contraction coupling fails. The measurable consequences are abnormal and asynchronous calcium transients and a loss of excitation-contraction coupling gain.

evidence.snippet: Cardiac-specific JPH2 knockdown resulted in impaired cardiac contractility, which caused heart failure and increased mortality.
evidence.explanation: Contractile failure and its outcome from an adult-onset, cardiac-restricted loss of the protein, which is the closest experimental analogue of the human recessive disease.

steps/4.description: Systolic dysfunction with ventricular dilation and progression to heart failure. In the acute knockdown mouse this is a direct and rapid consequence of losing junctophilin-2 in the adult heart, which matters for interpreting the human disease: it shows the protein is required continuously for contractile function, not only for building the dyad during development.

evidence.snippet: Family-based genetic analysis of GME individuals with cardiomyopathic disease identified an Iranian patient with dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM) as a carrier of a novel, homozygous single nucleotide insertion in JPH2 resulting in a stop codon (JPH2-p.E641*).
evidence.explanation: The phenotype in the index patient, tied to the homozygous allele.

evidence.snippet: In analyzing the 24 probands described in the studies, we found that autosomal recessive, loss-of-function variants are associated with severe, early onset DCM, while autosomal dominant missense variants are associated with a wider range of cardiac disease, including HCM, arrhythmia, SCD, and cardiac conduction disease.
evidence.explanation: Dilated cardiomyopathy as the phenotype of the recessive loss-of-function group specifically, which is what makes OBLIGATE defensible here: the genotype is defined by the phenotype it produces in this review's analysis.

steps/5.description: Ventricular dilation with systolic dysfunction, presenting in the neonatal period or early childhood. It is the defining phenotype of the entry.

evidence.snippet: A second Iranian family with consanguineous parents hosting an identical heterozygous variant had 2 children die in childhood from cardiac failure.
evidence.explanation: Cardiac failure as the cause of death in two affected children of a second family carrying the same allele.

steps/6.description: Progressive systolic heart failure, the clinical expression of the contractile defect and the cause of death in untreated affected children.

evidence.snippet: Cardiac myocytes from the mutant mice showed deficiency of the junctional membrane complexes and abnormal Ca2+ transients.
evidence.explanation: The structural and functional consequence of losing JP-2, in the same cells, which is what this edge asserts.

edges/1.description: Junctophilin-2 is the structural protein of the complex, so removing it prevents the complex from forming. Demonstrated in the germline null mouse, whose cardiomyocytes show deficient junctional membrane complexes.

evidence.snippet: Previously, missense variants in JPH2 have been linked to hypertrophic cardiomyopathy; however, pathogenic "loss of function" (LOF) variants have not been described.
evidence.explanation: States what was known before this report and what it added, which is the distinction between this entry and the dominant JPH2 disease.

evidence.snippet: Currently, ClinGen considers JPH2 to have moderate evidence for association with HCM in an autosomal dominant inheritance pattern, and moderate evidence for association with DCM in a semidominant inheritance pattern.
evidence.explanation: The curated gene-disease validity position for both phenotypes. Note the word for the DCM relationship is semidominant rather than recessive, which is a weaker claim than this entry's title makes and is why it is quoted rather than paraphrased.

evidence.snippet: The disease genes converge on metabolic causes (PRKAG2, MRPL44, AARS2, HADHB, DNAJC19, PPA2, TAZ, BAG3), MAPK pathways (HRAS, PTPN11, RAF1, TAB2), development (NEK8 and TBX20), calcium signaling (JPH2, CALM1, CACNA1C), and the sarcomeric contraction cycle (TNNC1, TNNI3, ACTC1, MYH7, NRAP)
evidence.explanation: Places JPH2 among the calcium-signalling causes of severe childhood cardiomyopathy in a countrywide cohort. This abstract does not describe the JPH2 kindred's allele; that detail is in the full text and is therefore not curated here.

genes/0.notes:
JPH2 encodes junctophilin-2, the structural protein of the cardiac dyad. One gene, two inheritance modes: biallelic loss of function causes this disease, and heterozygous missense variants cause hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, curated separately as Hypertrophic_Cardiomyopathy_17. ClinGen's position at the time of the systematic review was moderate evidence for JPH2 in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy with autosomal dominant inheritance and moderate evidence for dilated cardiomyopathy with semidominant inheritance.
A caution for anyone re-deriving this binding from a deep-research report: the OpenScientist run for this entry offered HGNC:14179 for JPH2. That identifier is CIAO3. The correct one, used here, is hgnc:14202, confirmed against the HGNC REST API. HGNC is skipped by the report's own term validator, so nothing in the pipeline would have caught it.

evidence.snippet: A second Iranian family with consanguineous parents hosting an identical heterozygous variant had 2 children die in childhood from cardiac failure.
evidence.explanation: The outcome without disease-modifying treatment, which is what supportive management is measured against here.

treatments/0.description: Standard heart failure care. There is no CMD2E-specific therapy, and the entry does not name individual agents because no source located reports a drug regimen in a genotyped CMD2E patient.

treatments/0/targets/0.description: Manages the failing circulation. It does not address the dyadic defect.

evidence.snippet: The KidCMP cohort presents remarkable early-onset and severe disorders: the median age of diagnosis was 0.33 years, and 17 patients underwent cardiac transplantation.
evidence.explanation: The transplantation count in the childhood cardiomyopathy cohort that includes JPH2 patients. It is a cohort figure and is labelled as one.

evidence.snippet: Genetic diagnoses may suggest intervention strategies and predict prognosis, offering valuable tools for prioritization of patients for transplantation versus conservative treatment.
evidence.explanation: The authors' argument that the genetic diagnosis itself informs the transplant decision, which is why molecular diagnosis is curated as consequential in a disease with no specific therapy.

treatments/1.description: Transplantation is a realistic endpoint in severe childhood-onset cardiomyopathy: 17 of 66 children in the Finnish countrywide cohort were transplanted. That figure is for the cohort, not for JPH2 patients.

treatments/1/targets/0.description: Replaces the failing heart, and with it the cardiomyocytes that lack junctophilin-2. It is the only intervention that removes the mechanism.

open_questions/0.rationale: The gene therapy result is real and striking: AAV9-JPH2 rescues contractility and preserves t-tubule structure in mice after transverse aortic constriction. But the model is not this disease. In transverse aortic constriction, junctophilin-2 falls secondarily as the heart fails, so the experiment restores a protein the animal once had, in a heart whose dyads were built normally. A CMD2E patient is a constitutive null whose dyads were never assembled, and whose myocardium has remodelled around their absence since before birth. Whether delivering junctophilin-2 to such a heart reassembles dyads, or arrives too late to reorganise a t-tubule system that never formed, is untested. The report treats this result as a strong preclinical rationale for CMD2E; that is a reasonable hope and it is not evidence, and the distinction matters because the patients are infants for whom transplantation is the alternative.

open_questions/1.rationale: This entry is titled and curated as autosomal recessive, and the segregation evidence in the Iranian kindred supports that. But ClinGen's curated position at the time of the systematic review was "semidominant" for the JPH2-dilated cardiomyopathy relationship, which is a different claim: it implies heterozygous carriers are not simply unaffected. Loss-of-function JPH2 variants are carried by 0.21% of Greater Middle Eastern individuals, so the carrier population is large enough to answer this, and none of the published work reports systematic cardiac phenotyping of heterozygous relatives. The stake is cascade screening: if carriers are at risk, the families already identified contain many people who should be under surveillance and are not.

evidence.snippet: All the MME mutations could be loss-of-function mutations, and we confirmed a lack/decrease of NEP protein expression in a peripheral nerve.
evidence.explanation: The Japanese biallelic cohort included direct sural-nerve protein observations; functional consequences of every individual allele were not experimentally established.

evidence.snippet: The sequences of RT‐PCR products revealed aberrantly spliced mRNA lacking exon 13, resulting in a loss of 99‐bp fragment (Fig. 3A).
evidence.explanation: Patient II:2 of the dHMN family B had the c.1416+2T>C splice allele. This is a blood-RNA observation in an allelic motor-predominant disorder.

evidence.snippet: However, the HEK293 cells transfected with c.1342C>T mutant contained only about 10% MME mRNA compared to that of wild‐type cells (Fig. 3D). Transcript levels could be increased after treatment with the translation inhibitor cycloheximide which blocks nonsense‐mediated mRNA decay.
evidence.explanation: The c.1342C>T nonsense-mediated-decay experiment used transfected HEK293 cells, separately from the nonsignificant lymphocyte transcript comparison.

evidence.snippet: The identified mutation causes a complete loss of carboxy-terminal region of the NEP protein which contains the zinc binding site and the catalytic domain and thus considered to be a loss-of-function mutation.
evidence.explanation: The p.Gln522* consequence was inferred from the stop-gain sequence and protein-domain location; this family study did not measure truncated protein or enzymatic activity.

steps/1.description: Germline biallelic pathogenic MME variants establish recessive disease; selected single variants can confer incompletely penetrant neuropathy susceptibility. Molecular effects are allele specific: patient RNA demonstrates exon skipping, transfected-cell experiments support nonsense-mediated decay and reduced synthetic-substrate cleavage for selected alleles, and other stop-gain or missense consequences remain predicted. Normal total lymphocyte transcript measurements in three dHMN patients do not exclude allele-specific RNA processing or loss of protein in nerve.

evidence.snippet: All the MME mutations could be loss-of-function mutations, and we confirmed a lack/decrease of NEP protein expression in a peripheral nerve.
evidence.explanation: The Japanese biallelic cohort included direct sural-nerve protein observations; functional consequences of every individual allele were not experimentally established.

evidence.snippet: Immunohistochemical stain with an anti‐MME antibody showed a mild decrease in positive reaction to nerve fibers (Fig. 4C) compared to the sural nerve from the control (Fig. 4D).
evidence.explanation: The biopsy was from dHMN family A patient II:2. Its mild protein reduction and preserved sensory-fiber structure differ from the severe sensory axon loss in other CMT2T biopsies.

evidence.snippet: The disease‐associated MME mutants showed significant decreases in MME enzymatic activity (Fig. 4F).
evidence.explanation: Activity was measured with a synthetic substrate in transfected HEK293 cells expressing c.1342C>T, c.2027C>T or c.2071_2072delGCinsTT; these alleles came from dHMN families. It was not an activity assay of the patient sural nerve.

steps/2.description: Absent or reduced neprilysin protein was demonstrated in sural nerve in recessive CMT2T. Reduction was mild in a sensory-nerve biopsy from a dHMN patient. Separate assays of selected mutant proteins in HEK293 cells establish impaired catalytic capacity, without demonstrating the activity of endogenous peptide substrates in patient nerve. Lower adipose-tissue and circulating protein levels in heterozygous cohorts provide additional, tissue-specific observations.

evidence.snippet: In our study, given that all patients with MME mutations showed late‐onset CMT, we believe that similar degeneration process may be present in both conditions by impairing Schwann cell–axonal interactions.
evidence.explanation: The authors propose impaired Schwann cell–axon interactions as a route to demyelination and axonal degeneration. This is a human-disease hypothesis, not a measured substrate or rescue experiment.

steps/3.description: Loss of neprilysin-mediated peptide processing is proposed to disturb support of peripheral axons by Schwann cells. Neprilysin localization in peripheral myelin and the human nerve lesions motivate this hypothesis, but no endogenous substrate has been shown to accumulate to a pathogenic concentration in CMT2T nerve. Young knockout mice repair a sciatic crush normally, limiting a simple universal remyelination-defect model; this result does not exclude all chronic human axon-support mechanisms.

evidence.snippet: showing 2 axonal clusters (arrows) with respectively 3 and 5 regenerating axons in 2 adjacent Schwann cells. Myelin fiber density is focally diminished.
evidence.explanation: Histological evidence of axonal loss with regeneration in patient sural nerve.

evidence.snippet: We observe a relatively mild axonal sensory-motor neuropathy with a greater impairment of the lower extremities.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the axonal character and the lower-limb predominance across a 32-patient series.

steps/4.description: Patient nerve biopsies show loss of myelinated axons with regenerative clusters; chronic neurogenic denervation and low motor/sensory response amplitudes provide complementary physiological evidence. The disease predominantly affects distal lower limbs, with upper-limb and sometimes proximal involvement as it progresses. Secondary myelin abnormalities can coexist. These findings support an axonal neuropathy substrate without making a named peptide or uniform Schwann-cell lesion its established cause.

evidence.snippet: Our findings indicate that AR-CMT2T caused by MME mutation predisposes to a superimposed inflammatory demyelinating neuropathy.
evidence.explanation: The authors infer inflammatory susceptibility from one case; this is not an observed penetrance estimate or proof that MME deficiency initiated inflammation.

evidence.snippet: The fragility of myelin sheath due to mutated neprilysin may trigger the detrimental immune response against peripheral myelin in this patient.
evidence.explanation: The proposed myelin-fragility-to-immunity route is explicitly hypothetical and specific to the reported patient.

steps/5.description: One homozygous MME patient developed an inflammatory demyelinating component with endoneurial edema, thinly myelinated fibers and a prompt clinical and electrophysiological response to immunoglobulin. The authors hypothesize that neprilysin-related myelin fragility predisposed to an immune response. Genetic predisposition is unproved, and other MME patients misdiagnosed with CIDP did not improve with immunomodulation.

evidence.snippet:
In the MME series, needle EMG revealed chronic neurogenic 
denervation. In some patients, positive sharp waves and fibril -
lation potentials were evident in the upper and lower limb 
muscles, particularly in the tibialis anterior muscle.
evidence.explanation: The biallelic series had chronic neurogenic denervation, with active spontaneous potentials in some patients. This supports motor-unit injury rather than a primary muscle disorder.

evidence.snippet: The electrophysiological and nerve conduction findings were consistent with chronic axonal sensorimotor polyneuropathy (predominantly motor) with active denervation.
evidence.explanation: The Iranian biallelic proband had motor-predominant axonal neuropathy with active denervation.

steps/6.description: Axonal motor nerve injury produces chronic neurogenic denervation in affected muscles. Electrophysiology demonstrates reduced recruitment and neurogenic motor-unit changes, sometimes with active spontaneous potentials. This supplies a clinical substrate for weakness and wasting; the molecular steps from neprilysin deficiency to motor axon injury remain incompletely resolved.

evidence.snippet: We observe a relatively mild axonal sensory-motor neuropathy with a greater impairment of the lower extremities.
evidence.explanation: The Italian clinical cohort shows lower-limb-predominant axonal neuropathy. Its 32 participants included 21 with pathogenic/likely pathogenic classifications, ten with uncertain variants and one with a likely benign variant; its mean severity is not universal disease severity.

steps/7.description: Progressive peripheral axonal neuropathy generally affects distal lower limbs first and can spread to the hands and proximal muscles. Motor and sensory involvement vary, and symptoms can range from subclinical sensory abnormalities to severe walking disability. Secondary demyelinating-range measurements do not exclude the diagnosis.

evidence.snippet: LL deep tendon reflexes (DTRs) are absent or reduced in 91% of patients, meanwhile UL DTRs are abnormal in 56%
evidence.explanation: These are the observed lower- and upper-limb rates in 32 Italian participants, including ten VUS and one likely benign classification. No P/LP-only denominator for this sign is supplied, so the whole-disease frequency is omitted.

evidence.snippet: distal sensory impairment, gait unsteadiness, and abolished ankle reflexes
evidence.explanation: Independent corroboration in a genotyped patient, and the basis for the description's statement that some patients have frank areflexia rather than only diminished reflexes.

steps/8.description: Tendon reflexes are reduced or absent, especially in the lower limbs, with generalized areflexia in some advanced patients. HP:0001315 covers the reduced-or-absent tendon-reflex spectrum. The Italian 91% lower-limb and 56% upper-limb figures describe a mixed variant-classification cohort and are retained as context rather than a disease-wide band.

evidence.snippet: Overall, 69% of patients show moderate to severe LL weakness while 81% show no or only mild strength deficit at the upper limb.
evidence.explanation: The 69% proportion is a severity-restricted lower-limb measurement in the mixed Italian cohort, not the occurrence rate of all distal weakness. The frequency band is omitted.

evidence.snippet: They showed muscle weakness, atrophy, and sensory disturbance in the lower extremities.
evidence.explanation: Documents distal weakness and atrophy in the defining series.

steps/9.description: Progressive distal weakness usually begins in the feet and lower legs and may later involve the hands. The Italian 69% figure measures moderate-to-severe lower-limb weakness, while 81% had no or only mild upper-limb deficit; it does not measure the prevalence of any distal weakness.

evidence.snippet: The patients suffered from vasomotor painful episodes and progressive gait disturbances and muscular weakness of the lower limbs with foot drop and frequent falls
evidence.explanation: The family follow-up describes foot drop among symptomatic patients. It does not establish the finding in every biallelic carrier.

steps/10.description: Weakness of foot dorsiflexors produces foot drop and contributes to walking difficulty and falls. The human phenotype is distinct from the compensatory steppage gait. Foot orthoses improved walking impairment and falls in Moroccan patient II:4.

evidence.snippet: Patient II:6 is a 34-year-old man who suffered from lower limb cramps and exercise intolerance since the age of 30 related to sensorimotor axonal PNP.
evidence.explanation: Direct clinical report of exercise intolerance attributed to sensorimotor axonal neuropathy in one genotyped patient.

steps/11.description: Exercise intolerance accompanied lower-limb cramps from age 30 in Moroccan patient II:6 and was attributed to his sensorimotor axonal neuropathy.

evidence.snippet: He currently shows typical symptoms of CMT including walking difficulty, bilateral foot drop, steppage gait, foot deformities (hammer toe), and loss of pain and temperature sensation in the lower parts of hands and feet.
evidence.explanation: The biallelic p.Gln522* proband VI.6 had steppage gait with foot drop and distal weakness.

steps/12.description: Steppage is a characteristic compensatory gait in patients with weak foot dorsiflexors. It was documented in the Iranian biallelic p.Gln522* family and in the European family follow-up.

evidence.snippet: with 62% reduced pinprick and 63% reduced light touch
evidence.explanation: The 62% pinprick and 63% light-touch deficits are different marginal rates. They do not determine the union of all distal sensory impairment, and the cohort includes VUS/likely benign findings; no general frequency band is inferred.

evidence.snippet: she presented with slight ataxia, distal sensory impairment, and gait unsteadiness
evidence.explanation: Documents distal sensory impairment as a presenting feature in a genotyped patient.

evidence.snippet: Muscle weakness is often associated with mild to moderate distal sensory loss.
evidence.explanation: The overview describes the general CMT clinical pattern. Primary MME cases establish occurrence here; no CMT-wide frequency, usual onset age or obligatory severity is transferred.

steps/13.description: Sensory loss affects distal limbs and can involve pain, temperature, vibration and joint-position perception. Some carriers have sensory abnormalities without symptoms, whereas motor-predominant patients may have little or no clinical sensory loss. The Italian pinprick and light-touch percentages describe separate modalities in a mixed variant cohort.

evidence.snippet: she presented with slight ataxia, distal sensory impairment, and gait unsteadiness
evidence.explanation: Documents gait unsteadiness in a genotyped patient.

steps/14.description: Unsteady gait and walking limitations occur with distal motor and sensory deficits. Some patients require orthoses or walking aids. Recurrent falls are represented separately.

evidence.snippet: she presented with slight ataxia, distal sensory impairment, and gait unsteadiness
evidence.explanation: Documents ataxia in a genotyped patient, and the word "slight" is what the MILD severity qualifier records. The source does not localise it.

steps/15.description: Portuguese patient III:3 had slight ataxia with distal sensory impairment and unsteady gait. The source did not distinguish sensory from cerebellar ataxia. The broad term and MILD qualifier preserve this observation; a qualified peripheral sensory explanation does not establish a cerebellar syndrome or transfer the separate SCA43 phenotype.

evidence.snippet: The patients suffered from vasomotor painful episodes and progressive gait disturbances and muscular weakness of the lower limbs with foot drop and frequent falls
evidence.explanation: The clinical family follow-up reports painful episodes among symptomatic patients. This is an occurrence statement, not a frequency estimate or proof of a single pain mechanism.

steps/16.description: Lower-limb pain and painful vasomotor episodes occur in some patients. Later cohorts also describe neuropathic pain, but neither all pain episodes nor every sensory symptom has been localized to a specific peptide or fiber population.

evidence.snippet: Patient II:6 is a 34-year-old man who suffered from lower limb cramps and exercise intolerance since the age of 30 related to sensorimotor axonal PNP.
evidence.explanation: The authors attribute cramps and exercise intolerance to the axonal sensorimotor neuropathy in Moroccan patient II:6; no disease-wide frequency follows from this case.

evidence.snippet:
The 
symptoms at the beginning of the disease were mainly motor, 
involving cramps and very frequent muscle contractures, 
although sensory symptoms were also prominent in the most 
evolved patients.
evidence.explanation: The Spanish authors describe cramps and muscle contractures in the biallelic cohort. These are clinical contraction symptoms; the wording alone does not establish fixed joint contractures.

steps/17.description: Cramps can precede or accompany weakness. They were attributed to sensorimotor axonal neuropathy in Moroccan patient II:6 and were frequent in the Spanish biallelic cohort.

evidence.snippet: He also complains of paresthesia in his fingers.
evidence.explanation: This patient-reported symptom belongs to biallelic p.Gln522* patient VI.2; it is not a measured sensory threshold.

steps/18.description: Paresthesia has been reported in distal limbs, including fingers in Iranian patient VI.2 and hands in a Dutch patient. It is a positive sensory symptom distinct from loss of sensation.

evidence.snippet: Typical pes cavus and distal lower limb amyotrophy exhibited by Patient II:4 and her brother Patient II:6, respectively, from the same Moroccan family.
evidence.explanation: The caption establishes pes cavus in II:4 only. Table 1 and the separate II:2 narrative establish the second positive among seven examined individuals: 2/7 = 28.6%, within OCCASIONAL. This small selected-cohort estimate is not a population prevalence.

steps/19.description: High-arched feet are documented in CMT2T but are not universal. Table 1 of the seven-person 2021 family series records pes cavus in two individuals (Moroccan II:2 and II:4), a selected sample ascertained through neonatal renal disease in offspring.

evidence.snippet: Typical pes cavus and distal lower limb amyotrophy exhibited by Patient II:4 and her brother Patient II:6, respectively, from the same Moroccan family.
evidence.explanation: The sentence attributes amyotrophy to Patient II:6 by the "respectively" construction, which is what this phenotype rests on; pes cavus above rests on the other half of the same sentence.

evidence.snippet: They showed muscle weakness, atrophy, and sensory disturbance in the lower extremities.
evidence.explanation: Documents atrophy alongside weakness in the defining recessive series.

steps/20.description: Distal muscle wasting affects the lower legs and feet and can extend to intrinsic hand muscles with progression. Proximal lower-limb atrophy is a separate reported finding.

evidence.snippet: His major problem is foot drop, frequent fall, gait steppage, and impaired sensation of temperature and pain in his fingers.
evidence.explanation: Biallelic patient VI.4 reported recurrent falls with foot drop and gait impairment.

genes/0.notes: MME encodes neprilysin, a membrane metallopeptidase with extracellular catalytic activity and multiple peptide substrates. Biallelic loss-of-function alleles establish recessive CMT2T; selected heterozygous variants confer incompletely penetrant neuropathy risk. RNA splicing and catalytic effects have been measured for particular alleles, while many truncation/NMD or structural effects remain predicted. Biallelic MME disease also includes a motor-predominant/dHMN spectrum, so sensory involvement is not obligatory. The 2024 Italian classifications describe 8 patients with pathogenic, 13 with likely pathogenic, 10 with uncertain and one with likely benign variants; these are patient counts, not 32 distinct variants. Diagnostic yield estimates derive from selected cohorts and do not establish an MME-first testing algorithm.

treatments/5.description: General CMT guidance recommends identifying the cause of pain before selecting symptomatic treatment. Musculoskeletal pain may respond to acetaminophen or nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory agents, whereas neuropathic pain may respond to tricyclic antidepressants, carbamazepine or gabapentin. These options are extrapolated from CMT-wide care, with no MME-specific efficacy claim; a reported painful limb is not automatically assigned a neuropathic pain mechanism.

evidence.explanation: The primary statement of the dominant mode and of its age-related incomplete penetrance.

evidence.snippet: Transmission of MME variants was often consistent with an incompletely penetrant autosomal-dominant trait and less frequently with autosomal-recessive inheritance.
evidence.explanation: The expanded cohort supports incompletely penetrant transmission; 51 patients overlapped with the original 2016 screening series.

evidence.snippet: This indicates that the heterozygous MME variants may not be fully penetrant, or alternatively, that they may be a potential risk factor for neuropathy.

evidence.explanation: The clause refers to tested heterozygous variants in the Spanish series. Nonsegregation directly challenges their causal interpretation; phenotypic diversity alone would not do so.

evidence.snippet: MME mutations that segregate in an autosomal recessive pattern are associated with a late-onset CMT2 phenotype, yet we could not demonstrate that MME variants in heterozygosis cause neuropathy.
evidence.explanation: The Spanish authors could not establish heterozygous causation in their families. This does not refute every allele in other populations.

open_questions/0.rationale: Biallelic pathogenic MME variants establish recessive neuropathy, while selected heterozygous variants segregate with disease and are enriched among late-onset neuropathy cohorts. The 2020 study already framed the latter as dominantly inherited susceptibility and partly reused the 2016 cohort. The Spanish series showed nonsegregation for tested heterozygous variants, with an alternative AIFM1 diagnosis for neuropathy/deafness and a pathogenic SOD1 variant in an ALS family. These findings are not evidence that every heterozygous allele causes disease. The 2024 Italian cohort contained 13 biallelic, 18 monoallelic and one unphased case, including ten VUS and one likely benign classification. Its Results describe the greater severity after ten years as not statistically significant because of an outlier, whereas the Discussion calls it significant; this cross-sectional contrast cannot establish an individual longitudinal progression rate. Age- and population-specific penetrance, modifying factors and variant-specific mechanisms remain unresolved.

evidence.snippet: In our study, given that all patients with MME mutations showed late‐onset CMT, we believe that similar degeneration process may be present in both conditions by impairing Schwann cell–axonal interactions.
evidence.explanation: The authors propose impaired Schwann cell–axon interactions as a route to demyelination and axonal degeneration. This is a human-disease hypothesis, not a measured substrate or rescue experiment.

evidence.explanation: The authors propose C-fiber dysfunction/degeneration and altered nociceptive-peptide processing as explanations for painful neuropathy. This is a qualified interpretation combining patient observations and mouse pathology.

evidence.snippet: However, contrary to the glomerular disease, which is immune mediated, the pathophysiology of the neuropathy is unknown.
evidence.explanation: This literature-status statement identifies the unresolved detailed mechanism, not absence of a causal association between MME deficiency and neuropathy.

open_questions/1.rationale: Human genotype/nerve-protein evidence establishes an etiological link to neuropathy, and the authors explicitly propose impaired Schwann cell–axon interactions. The relevant substrates and intervening molecular pathway are not established. Peptide turnover and nociceptive signaling remain candidates. Normal young-mouse repair after sciatic crush does not exclude every chronic support mechanism in humans. Negative amyloid PET in one Japanese patient and absent deposits in selected peripheral tissues do not exclude future dementia or every amyloid-related pathway; one biallelic Spanish patient developed late-life Alzheimer dementia. Onset varies substantially rather than invariably taking five decades.

evidence.snippet: Finally, we suggest that prolonged administration in patients with heart failure of an angiotensin receptor antagonist combined with a NEP inhibitor should include careful long-term neurological surveillance, although no adverse effect has been reported as yet, possibly for lack of sufficient hindsight.
evidence.explanation: Author recommendation for pharmacovigilance, explicitly acknowledging that no adverse effect had been observed; not a clinical toxicity observation.

evidence.snippet: Identification of MME-related Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease in families should lead to early screening of women predisposed to feto-maternal allo-immunization and renal complications in their offspring.
evidence.explanation: Author recommendation for reproductive family screening based on the established maternal alloimmunization context; not an outcome trial of screening.

open_questions/2.rationale: Maternal alloimmunization against neprilysin can cause membranous nephropathy in offspring of neprilysin-null women. The renal disease and neonatal deaths described in those pedigrees belong to the children and are not CMT2T maternal phenotypes. The source recommends family screening and long-term neurological vigilance during neprilysin-inhibitor therapy, while explicitly reporting no observed drug-associated adverse effect. These recommendations are not proof of treatment-induced neuropathy. The affected adults’ mild proteinuria in the Japanese cohort is a separate observation with unresolved attribution.

open_questions/3.rationale: One biallelic Spanish patient had Alzheimer dementia beginning at 67, but a patient with the same homozygous variant had no cognitive impairment. Negative cohort screening and single-patient PET observations do not establish lifetime absence. Neither a specific MME-mediated brain lesion nor excess age-adjusted dementia risk is demonstrated, so no causal edge is asserted. The Spanish dementia patient also had extensive diffuse white-matter damage; that table wording does not establish the multifocal hyperintensity pattern described in Iranian VI.4.

open_questions/4.rationale: Stuttering and multifocal high-signal white-matter foci were reported in one biallelic patient; the imaging differential included demyelination and chronic ischemia. The other affected relatives had normal brain imaging. A peripheral motor-unit lesion does not account for these findings without additional evidence. Cervical degenerative disc changes were also reported but are not established as an MME manifestation.

open_questions/6.rationale: Adult onset is typical but variable: symptomatic individuals in the 2021 family follow-up began between 30 and 43 years, while one 41-year-old carrier had subclinical findings. Spanish biallelic onset ranged from 35 to 73 years. The 2019 and 2024 Chinese reports describe a motor-predominant/dHMN allelic spectrum; the 2019 series includes onset at 16, so its abstract’s late-onset summary is not universal. Isolated finger contracture and hand tremor in those dHMN cases and a Babinski sign in the 2024 motor-predominant proband are not transferred automatically to the sensorimotor CMT2T annotation set. General wording about frequent muscle contractures in the Spanish report does not establish fixed joint contractures. The 2026 Iranian cohort reports a second DNA2 likely-pathogenic variant with rimmed-vacuole myopathic pathology in one case; that myopathy is not assigned to MME. Somatic or allelic non-neuropathy associations are not phenotype evidence for CMT2T. The Italian table separately labels age-associated, immune, vascular and neoplastic diagnoses as comorbidities; their occurrence does not establish MME manifestations. Fatigue in one biallelic patient is a nonspecific accompanying report and is not used as evidence for the distinct exercise-intolerance term.

steps/0.description: The proposed initiating mechanism is post-infectious molecular mimicry. An immunodominant peptide recognized by IgG from Cogan syndrome patients shares sequence similarity with the reovirus III major core protein and the SSA/Ro autoantigen, breaking immune tolerance and generating autoantibodies that cross-react with inner-ear and endothelial self-antigens (including CD148/DEP-1 and connexin 26). Infection may contribute, but autoimmunity is regarded as the primary driver; the pathogenesis remains incompletely defined.

steps/2.description: A CFTR genotype that reduces chloride and bicarbonate conductance without abolishing it. This is the defining feature of the disease and the reason it is not cystic fibrosis: the same gene, a different point on the residual- function axis. The threshold that matters is tissue-specific, and the mesonephric duct derivatives sit at the sensitive end of it - so a genotype that leaves lung and pancreas essentially normal still fails here.

steps/3.description: The alternative entry point. ADGRG2 is an adhesion GPCR expressed specifically in the epididymis and efferent ducts, where it is required for fluid reabsorption. Hemizygous truncating variants abolish it. That a receptor governing duct fluid handling and a channel governing duct fluid secretion both produce the same anatomical endpoint is the strongest argument that luminal fluid balance, rather than any one gene product, is what the mesonephric duct derivatives depend on.

evidence.snippet: It has also been demonstrated that fluid secretion is necessary for the normal development of the mesonephric duct
evidence.explanation: The link from secretion to duct development that this node turns on.

evidence.snippet: resulting in the production of highly viscous mucus by epithelial cells of the male genital tract
