evidence.snippet: MFN2 | HGNC:16877 | multiple symmetric lipomatosis with partial lipodystrophy | MONDO:1060153 | AR | Definitive
evidence.explanation: ClinGen curates MFN2 against a separate autosomal recessive disease term, not against a familial partial lipodystrophy term, which is the basis for not making MFN2 a subtype of this entry.

evidence.snippet: One specific MFN2 variant, p.Arg707Trp, has been reported in all multiple symmetric lipomatosis with partial lipodystrophy cases to date.
evidence.explanation: The single recurrent allele behind every reported case is part of what distinguishes this entity from the allelically heterogeneous FPLD subtypes.

genes/7.notes: Rare cases of partial lipodystrophy are associated with MFN2; identified in 0.9% of a genetically confirmed FPLD cohort. No subtype is assigned and relationship_type is left unset, because the entity ClinGen curates for MFN2 is not familial partial lipodystrophy: it is autosomal recessive multiple symmetric lipomatosis with partial lipodystrophy (MONDO:1060153, OMIM 151800), rated Definitive, in which every reported patient carries at least one p.Arg707Trp allele and upper-body adipose overgrowth accompanies the limb lipodystrophy. The inheritance also differs from the dominant FPLD forms curated above. MFN2 is retained on this entry because MFN2 carriers turn up in genetically screened FPLD cohorts and a curator reading an MFN2 result needs to find this disposition; it is a candidate for a separate dismech entry rather than an FPLD subtype.

evidence.snippet: Further analysis of WES data of 222 patients with unexplained FPL identified two unrelated patients with FPL with novel heterozygous (p.Cys1600Tyr and p.Gln1552Pro) NOTCH3 variants.
evidence.explanation: Two further unrelated probands beyond the index pedigree are the human genetic evidence for this gene-disease relationship, and also show how narrow it still is.

evidence.snippet: We conclude that gain-of-function missense variants in the negative regulatory region of NOTCH3 cause a novel subtype of FPL by activation of senescence pathways.
evidence.explanation: The authors' own conclusion, which describes the entity as a novel subtype of familial partial lipodystrophy rather than as the Koebberling type that OMIM and MONDO attach the gene to.

genes/8.notes: Heterozygous missense variants clustered in the heterodimerization domain of the NOTCH3 negative regulatory region were reported in three unrelated families with familial partial lipodystrophy, with patient fibroblasts showing raised NOTCH3 expression and activation of senescence pathways. No subtype is assigned. OMIM has folded this gene-disease relationship into phenotype MIM 608600 (familial partial lipodystrophy type 1, the Koebberling type), and MONDO therefore records NOTCH3 as the causal gene of MONDO:0012072; the source report instead describes its families as a novel subtype of FPL and does not call them Koebberling, so this entry curates the gene without asserting that equivalence (see the review_notes on the FPLD1 subtype). relationship_type is UNKNOWN: the evidence is a single 2025 publication, the ClinGen validity table committed in this repository has no NOTCH3 row for any lipodystrophy (its only NOTCH3 row is a Disputed pulmonary arterial hypertension curation), and that publication carries an erratum (PMID:41147879) whose content could not be retrieved - see the FPLD1 review_notes.

evidence.snippet: These findings establish PLAAT3 deficiency as a hereditary lipodystrophy syndrome with neurological manifestations, caused by a PPARγ-dependent defect in WAT differentiation and function.
evidence.explanation: The report's own conclusion establishing the gene-disease relationship and naming the PPARgamma-dependent mechanism wired on the pathophysiology graph.

genes/9.notes: Homozygous loss-of-function PLAAT3 variants were identified in seven patients from four unrelated consanguineous families with a lipodystrophy syndrome, with variable neurological involvement. The ClinGen validity table committed in this repository contains no PLAAT3 row, so the CAUSATIVE relationship_type rests on the primary report - multiple unrelated consanguineous families, a concordant mouse knockout, and CRISPR inactivation in human adipose stem cells - together with OMIM and MONDO recognition of the locus as FPLD9.

evidence.snippet: We conclude that heterozygous p.Leu68Phe ADRA2A mutation causes a rare atypical FPLD, most likely by inducing excessive lipolysis in some adipose tissue depots.
evidence.explanation: The founding report's own conclusion, giving both the allele and the proposed excessive-lipolysis mechanism curated on the pathophysiology node.

evidence.snippet: Conversely, increasing use of next-generation sequencing has led to proliferation of proposed new genetic causes of lipodystrophy with variable supporting evidence.
evidence.explanation: The ECLip consensus states the field-level reason this single-pedigree association is recorded with an UNKNOWN relationship_type rather than as causative.

genes/10.notes: A heterozygous ADRA2A p.Leu68Phe variant segregated with atypical familial partial lipodystrophy in a single African-American pedigree; functional work in the same report showed the mutant receptor produced more cAMP and glycerol and was resistant to alpha-2 agonist and antagonist, consistent with loss of the receptor's normal restraint on adipocyte lipolysis. OMIM numbers this FPLD8 (620679) and MONDO carries it as MONDO:0958022. relationship_type is UNKNOWN: the evidence is one pedigree, the ClinGen validity table committed in this repository contains no ADRA2A row, and the European Consortium for Lipodystrophies consensus warns that next-generation sequencing has produced a proliferation of proposed new genetic causes of lipodystrophy with variable supporting evidence.

treatments/0.description: Balanced calorie-controlled diet (typically ~50-60% carbohydrate, 20-30% fat, ~20% protein) with reduced simple sugars and alcohol abstinence to reduce metabolic stress on limited adipose storage capacity and lower triglyceride/pancreatitis risk.

treatments/1.description: Regular aerobic exercise (after cardiac evaluation) to improve insulin sensitivity and cardiometabolic risk.

treatments/2.description: First-line pharmacotherapy for hyperglycemia and insulin resistance in FPLD.

treatments/3.description: First-line lipid-lowering therapy (e.g., atorvastatin) for dyslipidemia.

treatments/4.description: Fibrates (e.g., fenofibrate), often with omega-3 fatty acids, for severe hypertriglyceridemia (TG > 500 mg/dL) to reduce pancreatitis risk.

treatments/5.description: Recombinant leptin analog (leptin replacement therapy); a major advance for generalized lipodystrophy, with more variable benefit in partial forms, associated with reductions in triglycerides and HbA1c in hypoleptinemic patients.

evidence.snippet: Our study demonstrates the relative safety and effectiveness of GLP-1RA in patients with FPLD.
evidence.explanation: Retrospective study supporting GLP-1RA efficacy and relative safety in FPLD, with a noted pancreatitis signal on longer therapy.

treatments/6.description: Glucagon-like peptide 1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RA) improve weight, BMI, HbA1c, fasting glucose, and triglycerides in FPLD; acute pancreatitis has been reported with longer therapy, warranting caution in patients with prior pancreatitis.

treatments/7.description: ApoC-III antisense oligonucleotide investigated for severe hypertriglyceridemia in FPLD (BROADEN trial); produces large triglyceride reductions.

treatments/8.description: Genetic counseling and cascade genetic testing of relatives are recommended for affected families.

evidence.snippet: Here we report mutations in the gene encoding the facilitative glucose transporter 2 (GLUT2) in three FBS families, including the original patient described in 1949 by Fanconi and Bickel.
evidence.explanation: The seminal gene-discovery study identifies SLC2A2/GLUT2 mutations as the molecular cause of Fanconi-Bickel syndrome, including in the original 1949 patient.

evidence.snippet: Genetic analysis revealed five distinct SLC2A2 pathogenic variants, including three previously unreported variants: p.Gln23Arg (c.68A > G), p.Thr353Arg (c.1058_1059delinsGG), and an exon 7 deletion.
evidence.explanation: A large Palestinian cohort study expands the SLC2A2 pathogenic variant spectrum, including novel missense variants and an exonic deletion.

steps/1.description: Biallelic pathogenic variants in SLC2A2, the gene encoding the facilitative glucose transporter GLUT2, predict truncated or non-functional translation products lacking monosaccharide transport activity. Reported variants include frameshift, nonsense, splice-site, and missense changes, as well as exonic deletions, distributed throughout the gene.

evidence.snippet: Fanconi-Bickel syndrome (FBS) is a rare autosomal recessive disorder of carbohydrate metabolism recently demonstrated to be caused by mutations in Glut2, the gene for the glucose transporter protein 2 expressed in liver, pancreas, intestine and kidney.
evidence.explanation: Describes GLUT2 expression across the four tissues (liver, pancreas, intestine, kidney) whose dysfunction defines the disease.

evidence.snippet: Renal proximal tubulopathy in Fanconi-Bickel syndrome is caused by impaired basolateral glucose transport via GLUT2 and consequently, intracellular accumulation of glucose and glycogen.
evidence.explanation: Directly links impaired basolateral GLUT2-mediated glucose transport to intracellular glucose/glycogen accumulation in renal proximal tubular cells.

steps/2.description: GLUT2 is a high-capacity, low-affinity facilitative glucose transporter normally expressed on the basolateral membrane of hepatocytes and renal proximal tubular epithelial cells, on pancreatic beta cells, and on the basolateral membrane of intestinal enterocytes, where it mediates bidirectional, insulin-independent glucose (and galactose) flux down the concentration gradient. Loss of GLUT2 activity uncouples intracellular glucose handling from these tissues' normal transport function, impairing both glucose uptake/release across the basolateral membrane and pancreatic beta-cell glucose sensing.

evidence.snippet: Fanconi-Bickel syndrome (FBS) is a rare autosomal-recessive inborn error of metabolism characterized by hepatorenal glycogen accumulation, Fanconi nephropathy and impaired utilization of glucose and galactose.
evidence.explanation: Establishes hepatorenal glycogen accumulation as a defining biochemical feature linked to the GLUT2 transport defect.

steps/3.description: With hepatocyte GLUT2 nonfunctional, glucose entering via other routes (e.g., during feeding) cannot be efficiently released back into the circulation during fasting, and instead accumulates intracellularly where it drives excessive glycogen synthesis. This produces massive hepatic glycogen accumulation and hepatomegaly, with impaired hepatic glucose output during fasting.

evidence.snippet: Renal proximal tubulopathy in Fanconi-Bickel syndrome is caused by impaired basolateral glucose transport via GLUT2 and consequently, intracellular accumulation of glucose and glycogen.
evidence.explanation: Directly links the renal Fanconi-type tubulopathy to impaired basolateral GLUT2-mediated glucose transport.

steps/4.description: Failure of basolateral GLUT2-mediated glucose efflux in the proximal tubule causes intracellular glucose and glycogen accumulation in tubular epithelial cells, producing a generalized (Fanconi-type) proximal tubulopathy characterized by glucosuria, generalized aminoaciduria, phosphaturia, and bicarbonaturia, despite normal or low blood glucose.

evidence.snippet: a characteristic proximal tubular nephropathy
evidence.explanation: Long-term natural history study identifies the characteristic proximal tubular (Fanconi-type) nephropathy as persisting into adulthood.

steps/5.description: Generalized proximal renal tubular dysfunction with glucosuria, generalized aminoaciduria, phosphaturia, and bicarbonaturia, caused by impaired basolateral renal tubular GLUT2 function.

evidence.snippet: Because all detected mutations (delta T446-449, C1251T and C1405T) predict truncated translation products that cannot be expected to have functional monosaccharide transport activity, GLUT2 mutations are probably the cause of FBS.
evidence.explanation: The gene-discovery study directly links the identified truncating mutations to loss of functional GLUT2 monosaccharide transport activity.

edges/2.description: Truncating and other loss-of-function SLC2A2 variants abolish GLUT2 monosaccharide transport activity.

evidence.snippet: hepatomegaly secondary to glycogen accumulation, glucose and galactose intolerance, fasting hypoglycaemia, a characteristic proximal tubular nephropathy and severe short stature
evidence.explanation: Long-term natural history study links hepatomegaly and glycogen accumulation to the underlying glucose transport defect.

edges/3.description: Loss of hepatocyte basolateral GLUT2 function traps glucose within hepatocytes, shifting it toward glycogen synthesis rather than release into the circulation.

evidence.snippet: Renal proximal tubulopathy in Fanconi-Bickel syndrome is caused by impaired basolateral glucose transport via GLUT2 and consequently, intracellular accumulation of glucose and glycogen.
evidence.explanation: Directly attributes the renal Fanconi-type tubulopathy to impaired basolateral GLUT2 transport and consequent intracellular glucose/glycogen accumulation.

edges/4.description: Loss of basolateral GLUT2 in renal proximal tubular epithelial cells impairs glucose exit from the reabsorbing cell back into the bloodstream, causing intracellular glucose and glycogen accumulation and secondary generalized proximal tubular dysfunction.

evidence.snippet: a characteristic proximal tubular nephropathy
evidence.explanation: Long-term natural history study identifies the characteristic proximal tubular nephropathy persisting into adulthood.

edges/5.description: Intracellular glucose/glycogen accumulation and consequent tubular cell dysfunction produce the generalized proximal reabsorptive defect characteristic of renal Fanconi syndrome.

evidence.snippet: Here we report mutations in the gene encoding the facilitative glucose transporter 2 (GLUT2) in three FBS families, including the original patient described in 1949 by Fanconi and Bickel.
evidence.explanation: The seminal gene-discovery study establishes SLC2A2/GLUT2 as the causative gene for Fanconi-Bickel syndrome.

evidence.snippet: Genetic analysis revealed five distinct SLC2A2 pathogenic variants, including three previously unreported variants: p.Gln23Arg (c.68A > G), p.Thr353Arg (c.1058_1059delinsGG), and an exon 7 deletion.
evidence.explanation: A large cohort study confirms and expands the SLC2A2 pathogenic variant spectrum causative for Fanconi-Bickel syndrome.

evidence.snippet: fasting hypoglycaemia
evidence.explanation: Long-term natural history study documents persistent fasting hypoglycemia, the target abnormality that frequent feeding/cornstarch dietary management addresses.

treatments/0.description: Frequent small meals and uncooked cornstarch supplementation provide a sustained-release glucose source to reduce the amplitude of fasting hypoglycemia and glucose/galactose intolerance characteristic of Fanconi-Bickel syndrome; galactose restriction is also used given the shared GLUT2-dependent transport defect.

treatments/0/targets/0.description: Frequent feeding and sustained-release cornstarch reduce the amplitude of glycemic instability resulting from impaired GLUT2-mediated hepatic glucose buffering and glucose/galactose intolerance.

evidence.snippet: supplementations (i.e., phosphate, alkali, carnitine, and alfacalcidol) could be completely discontinued in the three children
evidence.explanation: Documents standard supplementation regimen (phosphate, alkali, carnitine, alfacalcidol) used to manage the renal tubulopathy prior to empagliflozin repurposing.

treatments/1.description: Oral phosphate, alkali, and active vitamin D (alfacalcidol) replacement address the renal phosphate and bicarbonate wasting from the proximal tubulopathy and support treatment of hypophosphatemic rickets.

treatments/1/targets/0.description: Supplementation replaces phosphate and bicarbonate lost through the Fanconi-type proximal tubulopathy and supports bone mineralization.

evidence.snippet: SGLT2 inhibitors such as empagliflozin shift the metabolic block in Fanconi-Bickel syndrome, that is, they intervene specifically in the underlying pathophysiology and can thus attenuate renal proximal tubulopathy, especially when started in early childhood.
evidence.explanation: A case series of seven genetically confirmed FBS patients demonstrates that empagliflozin, by blocking apical tubular glucose reabsorption, specifically targets the underlying basolateral GLUT2 transport defect and improves biochemical markers of tubular function.

evidence.snippet: biochemical parameters of tubular cell integrity (urinary N-acetyl-glucosaminidase) and/or tubular functions (including urinary α1-microglobulin) improved in all persons with Fanconi-Bickel syndrome, albeit to varying degrees
evidence.explanation: Demonstrates measurable improvement in tubular cell integrity and function biomarkers under empagliflozin treatment across all seven treated patients.

treatments/2.description: Off-label repurposing of the SGLT2 inhibitor empagliflozin blocks apical glucose reabsorption in renal proximal tubular cells, reducing the intracellular glucose/glycogen burden created by the basolateral GLUT2 defect and improving biochemical markers of tubular integrity and function; in a case series, phosphate/alkali/carnitine/alfacalcidol supplementation could be discontinued in treated children.

treatments/2/targets/0.description: SGLT2 inhibition blocks apical glucose reabsorption in the proximal tubule, shifting the metabolic block and reducing the intracellular glucose/glycogen accumulation caused by the basolateral GLUT2 defect.

evidence.snippet: avascularity of articular cartilage and the limited ability to proliferate and promote repair
evidence.explanation: Establishes the focal chondral lesion of the knee as a structural cartilage injury in a tissue with intrinsically limited repair capacity.

evidence.snippet: The management of OCL is predicated on certain injury characteristics, including lesion location and the extent of subchondral disease
evidence.explanation: Confirms that lesion location and subchondral bone involvement define the osteochondral injury and drive management, supporting the chondral-versus-osteochondral distinction.

steps/0.description: An acute traumatic shear/impact load, osteochondritis dissecans, or repetitive microtrauma produces a discrete full-thickness defect of the hyaline articular cartilage, disrupting the smooth load-bearing joint surface while leaving the surrounding cartilage relatively intact. The lesion may be purely chondral or osteochondral when it extends into the subchondral bone; because the cartilage and its supporting subchondral plate function together as an osteochondral unit, the extent of subchondral disease shapes both the mechanical consequences and the choice of restoration procedure.

evidence.snippet: Articular cartilage has very little capacity for self-repair, so damage may be permanent
evidence.explanation: Directly supports the core mechanism that a focal full-thickness defect does not heal because of the limited intrinsic repair capacity of hyaline cartilage.

steps/1.description: Mature hyaline articular cartilage is avascular, alymphatic, and aneural, and its resident chondrocytes are entrapped in a dense matrix with little capacity to proliferate or migrate into a defect. Consequently a full-thickness chondral lesion has minimal intrinsic self-repair and the damage is frequently permanent.

evidence.snippet: produce only fibrocartilage and therefore do not offer a long-term cure
evidence.explanation: Supports that marrow-stimulation repair of chondral defects yields biomechanically inferior fibrocartilage rather than durable hyaline cartilage.

steps/2.description: When repair does occur — spontaneously or after marrow-stimulation procedures (microfracture, drilling, abrasion arthroplasty) — bone-marrow mesenchymal stromal cells populate the defect and produce type I collagen-rich fibrocartilage rather than type II collagen hyaline cartilage. This fibrocartilage is biomechanically inferior and degrades over time, so it does not durably restore the articular surface.

evidence.snippet: Untreated lesions can lead to early development of arthritis and the need for joint replacement
evidence.explanation: Supports the causal link from an untreated focal cartilage defect to secondary osteoarthritis and eventual arthroplasty.

steps/3.description: An untreated or inadequately repaired focal chondral defect concentrates mechanical stress on adjacent cartilage and subchondral bone, promoting progressive cartilage loss that converges on the degenerative phenotype of secondary osteoarthritis and may ultimately require joint replacement. This is post-traumatic osteoarthritis: the focal lesion is the discrete injury that imposes the abnormal mechanical loading and chondrocyte stress program captured by the conserved osteoarthritis degradation module, motivating early restoration of the articular surface.

edges/0.description: A full-thickness defect in avascular hyaline cartilage cannot recruit a normal vascular healing response.

edges/1.description: In the absence of true hyaline regeneration, any spontaneous or marrow-derived fill is fibrocartilaginous rather than hyaline.

edges/2.description: A persistent unrepaired surface defect alters joint load distribution and drives degenerative change.

edges/3.description: Inferior fibrocartilage degrades under load, leaving the joint surface vulnerable to degenerative progression.

evidence.snippet: MACI offers a more efficacious alternative than MFX with a similar safety profile for the treatment of symptomatic articular cartilage defects of the knee
evidence.explanation: Randomized controlled evidence that MACI is efficacious for symptomatic focal cartilage defects of the knee.

treatments/0.description: Two-stage autologous cell therapy for symptomatic full-thickness cartilage defects of the knee. Chondrocytes are arthroscopically harvested, expanded in culture, and seeded onto a porcine type I/III collagen membrane that is implanted into the debrided defect to regenerate hyaline-like cartilage. In the randomized SUMMIT trial, MACI was clinically and statistically superior to microfracture for symptomatic defects of the knee. MACI is indicated for focal cartilage defects, not for generalized osteoarthritis.

treatments/0/targets/0.description: MACI implants cultured autologous chondrocytes to regenerate hyaline-like cartilage, directly compensating for the cartilage's failed intrinsic repair.

evidence.snippet: produce only fibrocartilage and therefore do not offer a long-term cure
evidence.explanation: Marrow-stimulation techniques relieve symptoms but generate fibrocartilage rather than durable hyaline repair.

treatments/1.description: A single-stage arthroscopic marrow-stimulation procedure in which small perforations are made in the subchondral bone to recruit marrow mesenchymal cells into the defect. It is technically simple and lower cost but produces biomechanically inferior fibrocartilage and is generally less durable than cell-based repair for larger defects.

treatments/1/targets/0.description: Perforating the subchondral plate recruits marrow mesenchymal cells into the defect, bypassing the avascular cartilage's failed intrinsic repair, but the resulting fill is fibrocartilage.

evidence.snippet: chondral lesions that involve a larger area or depth require restorative procedures such as osteochondral allograft transplantation or other cell-based techniques
evidence.explanation: Supports osteochondral allograft transplantation as the restorative approach for larger or deeper focal chondral lesions.

treatments/2.description: Transplantation of size-matched donor osteochondral plugs (mature hyaline cartilage on a supporting bone base) into the debrided defect. It is a restorative option reserved for larger or deeper lesions and osteochondral defects involving the subchondral bone, where surface-based or marrow-stimulation techniques are less durable.

treatments/2/targets/0.description: A mature osteochondral graft physically replaces the defect, restoring the articular surface and, for osteochondral lesions, the underlying subchondral bone.

treatments/2/targets/1.description: Transplanting pre-formed mature hyaline cartilage bypasses the need for intrinsic repair the host cartilage cannot achieve.

evidence.snippet: The OAT technique for ACD or OCD repair in the athletic population allows for a higher rate of return to and maintenance of sports at the preinjury level compared with MF
evidence.explanation: A 10-year randomized controlled trial supports osteochondral autograft transfer as superior to microfracture for return to sport after focal osteochondral defects.

treatments/3.description: Transfer of one or more autologous osteochondral plugs harvested from a low-weightbearing region of the knee into the defect, restoring the surface with the patient's own mature hyaline cartilage. It is generally used for smaller focal osteochondral lesions. A 10-year randomized trial in athletes found OAT gave higher rates of return to and maintenance of preinjury-level sport than microfracture.

treatments/3/targets/0.description: Autologous osteochondral plugs physically restore the cartilage (and subchondral) surface at the defect.

treatments/3/targets/1.description: Grafting mature autologous hyaline cartilage bypasses the cartilage's failed intrinsic repair.

evidence.snippet: Type 0 glycogen storage disease (GSD0) is caused by deficiency of the hepatic isoform of glycogen synthase.
evidence.explanation: Names the enzymatic lesion and, importantly, its isoform - the hepatic one, not the muscle isoform whose deficiency is a different disease.

evidence.snippet: GS activity in the liver of the affected children was extremely low or nil, resulting in subnormal glycogen content.
evidence.explanation: Measures the enzyme deficiency directly in liver tissue and states its immediate consequence for glycogen content.

steps/1.description: Biallelic GYS2 loss of function removes the liver isoform of glycogen synthase, the enzyme that transfers glucose from UDP-glucose onto the growing alpha-1,4 chain. This is the synthesis-side counterpart of the phosphorylase lesion in GSD VI: the same polymer, the opposite direction of the reaction, and therefore the opposite tissue consequence. Liver enzyme activity in affected children is extremely low or unmeasurable.

evidence.snippet: In contrast to the other GSDs that are associated with glycogen accumulation, GSD 0 is characterized by an extremely low amount of glycogen in hepatocytes.
evidence.explanation: States the cellular consequence and, in the same sentence, its inversion of the rest of the glycogenoses.

steps/2.description: Hepatocytes cannot polymerise incoming glucose into glycogen. Two consequences branch from this one node, and holding both in view is what makes the disease legible: the liver has no glycogen reserve to draw on when fasting, and it has nowhere to put dietary glucose when fed. Everything downstream is one of those two branches.

evidence.snippet: Glucose and other sugars taken up by the liver in GSD0 are shunted into the glycolytic pathway leading to postprandial hyperlactatemia and hyperlipidemia
evidence.explanation: Names the shunt itself and both of its measurable consequences, lactate and lipid.

evidence.snippet: Because a substantial fraction of dietary carbohydrate is normally stored in the liver as glycogen
evidence.explanation: Supplies the quantitative premise the shunt rests on: the missing sink is large enough for its loss to change systemic glucose handling.

steps/3.description: The fed half of the disease, and the part that is most often misread. A substantial fraction of dietary carbohydrate is normally parked in hepatic glycogen; with that sink removed, glucose and other sugars taken up by the liver are diverted into glycolysis. The liver therefore converts a meal into lactate instead of into stored polymer.

evidence.snippet: The glycogen synthase (GS) activity has been low or immeasurable in liver biopsies, whereas the liver glycogen content has been only moderately decreased.
evidence.explanation: The calibrating observation for this node: enzyme activity is essentially absent while glycogen content is only moderately reduced, which is why this entry does not claim zero hepatic glycogen.

evidence.snippet: In contrast to all other types of glycogenoses, which are characterized by increased glycogen storage, deficiency of glycogen synthase causes a marked decrease in liver glycogen content.
evidence.explanation: Grades the depletion as marked and states the contrast with the rest of the group.

steps/4.description: The liver holds subnormal glycogen. Note the calibration: the classic descriptions say markedly decreased rather than absent, and the original linkage study reported the content as only moderately decreased despite enzyme activity being nil - residual glycogen presumably reflects other minor routes of glucosyl transfer, so "no glycogen at all" would overstate it. The functional point is that the reserve is too small to buffer a fast, and too small to enlarge the organ.

evidence.snippet: GSD0 is the only GSD not associated with hepatomegaly, and hypoglycemia typically is milder than in the other types of GSD.
evidence.explanation: States both halves of what makes this node discriminating - uniquely no hepatomegaly, and milder hypoglycemia than the storage-side diseases.

evidence.snippet: The diagnosis of GSD0 should be considered in a child with ketotic fasting hypoglycemia with postprandial hyperglycemia but without hepatomegaly.
evidence.explanation: Frames absent hepatomegaly as a positive part of the diagnostic triad rather than merely a missing feature.

steps/5.description: A negative finding curated as a node because it is load-bearing rather than incidental. Every other hepatic glycogenosis presents with an enlarged liver, and it is the absence of hepatomegaly that keeps GSD 0a out of the differential in a child with fasting hypoglycemia. This node is the reason the disease is missed.

evidence.snippet: Intact gluconeogenesis and fatty acid oxidation blunt the decrease in blood glucose levels in the postabsorptive period and explains why this disorder is typically milder than the other hepatic glycogenoses.
evidence.explanation: Establishes both preserved pathways and ties their preservation to the comparative mildness of the fasting phenotype.

steps/6.description: In the postabsorptive state the liver has almost no glycogen to mobilise, so hepatic glucose output rests entirely on gluconeogenesis. Both gluconeogenesis and fatty-acid oxidation are intact here - the lesion is confined to the synthetic step - and their preservation is what keeps the hypoglycemia milder than in GSD I while simultaneously making it ketotic.

evidence.snippet: The disorder is characterized by hyperketotic hypoglycemia without hyperlactatemia after fasting.
evidence.explanation: States the fasting combination with the explicit negative - hyperketosis WITHOUT hyperlactatemia.

evidence.snippet: The disorder is characterized by fasting hyperketotic hypoglycemia without hyperalaninemia or hyperlactacidemia.
evidence.explanation: Independently states the same fasting signature and adds the absent hyperalaninemia.

evidence.snippet: Fasting hypoglycemia usually manifests in late infancy when overnight feedings are stopped.
evidence.explanation: Supplies the timing: the fast only becomes long enough to unmask the defect when night feeds stop.

steps/7.description: The fasted half of the disease. Glucose falls, ketones rise, and - this is the discriminating detail - lactate and alanine are LOW rather than high. Low lactate follows from gluconeogenesis running at full tilt and consuming lactate as substrate, and low alanine from its consumption as a gluconeogenic precursor; both are the mirror image of GSD I, where the gluconeogenic block dams lactate up and produces fasting lactic acidosis. Symptoms typically surface in late infancy, when overnight feeds are dropped.

evidence.snippet: With more prolonged fasting, however, severe hyperketonemia and free fatty acid elevation inhibit release of alanine from skeletal muscle leading to decreased gluconeogenic precursors and worsening hypoglycemia.
evidence.explanation: Describes the loop end to end - ketones and fatty acids suppressing alanine release, precursor supply falling, hypoglycemia worsening.

steps/8.description: An amplifying loop that explains why a fast that is tolerated for hours can decompensate abruptly. Severe hyperketonemia and elevated free fatty acids suppress alanine release from skeletal muscle; alanine is the principal gluconeogenic precursor, and gluconeogenesis is the only remaining route to hepatic glucose output. The compensation that keeps this disease mild is therefore self-limiting.

evidence.snippet: Although feeding relieves symptoms, it often results in postprandial hyperglycemia and hyperlactatemia.
evidence.explanation: Records the paradox at the centre of this node - the treatment for the fasted state produces the fed-state abnormality.

evidence.snippet: This patient presented with fasting ketotic hypoglycaemia associated with postprandial hyperglycaemia and elevated lactate level.
evidence.explanation: A genetically confirmed patient in whom the fed and fasted abnormalities were documented together.

steps/9.description: After a carbohydrate meal, blood glucose rises abnormally and lactate rises with it. Both directions of the day are thus abnormal in opposite ways, which is why single fasting or single random measurements mislead: a fed sample looks like early diabetes mellitus, a fasted sample looks like idiopathic ketotic hypoglycemia, and only the pair identifies the disease.

evidence.snippet: We describe two children with GSD0, confirmed by mutation analysis, who had glucosuria and hyperglycemia.
evidence.explanation: Documents glucosuria co-occurring with hyperglycemia in molecularly confirmed patients, which is the observation this node explains.

steps/10.description: Postprandial glucose high enough to exceed the renal tubular reabsorption threshold produces glucosuria with normal kidneys. This is the step that makes GSD 0a reachable from a dipstick abnormality rather than from a hypoglycemia workup, and it is why the disease has been picked up during evaluation of apparent early diabetes.

evidence.snippet: Glucose monitoring in both patients revealed daily fluctuations from fasting hypoglycemia to postprandial hyperglycemia and lactic acidemia.
evidence.explanation: Directly documents the daily oscillation, including its lactate component, by serial monitoring in two siblings.

evidence.snippet: Glucose monitoring in both patients revealed daily fluctuations from fasting hypoglycemia to postprandial hyperglycemia.
evidence.explanation: An independent pair of patients showing the same daily swing, from the earlier report by the same group.

evidence.snippet: The disorder is clinically characterized by ketotic fasting hypoglycemia in combination with postprandial hyperglycemia and hyperlactatemia.
evidence.explanation: States the combination as the defining clinical characterisation, not as a coincidence of two findings.

steps/11.description: The integrating node, and the diagnostic signature of the disease. Because the liver can neither store glucose when fed nor release it when fasted, glycemia swings across the day between postprandial hyperglycemia with lactic acidemia and fasting ketotic hypoglycemia, instead of being buffered flat. Continuous or serial glucose monitoring shows daily fluctuation between the two poles; neither pole alone is specific, and it is the oscillation that is.

evidence.snippet: fasting hypoglycemia and ketonuria are universal in children less than 5 years of age
evidence.explanation: A universal finding in the under-fives supports a VERY_FREQUENT band; the qualifier is set to NOCTURNAL because the episodes are described as overnight, appearing when night feeds stop.

evidence.snippet: Most children over 7 years of age tolerate a typical overnight fast without development of hypoglycemia, and fasting for up to 18 hours has been reported in teenagers.
evidence.explanation: Records the age-dependence, which qualifies the frequency band: it applies to young children, not to the whole lifespan.

steps/12.description: Fasting hypoglycemia accompanied by ketosis, emerging on the overnight fast once night feeds are dropped. The accompanying lactate is low, not high, which is the feature that separates it from the hypoglycemia of GSD I. Fasting tolerance generally improves with age.

evidence.snippet: Glycogen storage disease type 0 (GSD 0) is an autosomal recessive disorder of glycogen metabolism caused by mutations in the GYS2 gene manifesting in infancy or early childhood and characterized by ketotic hypoglycemia after prolonged fasting, and postprandial hyperglycemia and hyperlactatemia.
evidence.explanation: Lists postprandial hyperglycemia among the characterising features, in the same sentence that pairs it with the fasting abnormality.

evidence.snippet: The second patient presented at 14 months with asymptomatic incidental hyperglycemia.
evidence.explanation: A patient whose presenting abnormality was the fed-state one, showing that hyperglycemia can be the entry point rather than a secondary detail.

steps/13.description: Blood glucose rises abnormally after a carbohydrate meal because the liver cannot clear the load into glycogen. The finding is easily read as early diabetes mellitus, and children have been referred for exactly that.

evidence.snippet: Although feeding relieves symptoms, it often results in postprandial hyperglycemia and hyperlactatemia.
evidence.explanation: Ties the lactate rise specifically to feeding, which is what the postprandial qualifier encodes.

evidence.snippet: Sequencing of the GYS2 gene is more likely to be positive in patients with fasting ketotic hypoglycaemia and concomitant postprandial hyperglycaemia with hyperlactataemia.
evidence.explanation: Gives the finding diagnostic weight: postprandial hyperlactataemia is what raises the pre-test probability of a GYS2 result.

steps/14.description: Lactate rises AFTER meals, not during fasting. The temporal direction is the whole discriminating value: GSD I produces fasting lactic acidosis from a gluconeogenic block, while here fasting lactate is low and the rise is confined to the fed state.

evidence.snippet: We describe two children with GSD0, confirmed by mutation analysis, who had glucosuria and hyperglycemia.
evidence.explanation: Two molecularly confirmed children with glucosuria; the band is set OCCASIONAL because these are reported as an unusual presentation within a literature of fewer than thirty cases.

evidence.snippet: GSD0 should be considered in any child with asymptomatic hyperglycemia or glucosuria.
evidence.explanation: Independently endorses glucosuria as an entry point to the diagnosis.

steps/15.description: Glucose in the urine when postprandial glycemia exceeds the renal threshold, with structurally normal kidneys. Reported as a presenting abnormality, and the reason the disease belongs in the differential of unexplained glucosuria as well as of ketotic hypoglycemia.

evidence.snippet: fasting hypoglycemia and ketonuria are universal in children less than 5 years of age
evidence.explanation: A universal finding in the under-fives supports the VERY_FREQUENT band for that age group.

steps/16.description: Ketone bodies in the urine during fasting, described as universal in children under five and the basis for home urine-ketone screening.

evidence.snippet: Seizures associated with low blood glucose may also occur, but they are rare.
evidence.explanation: States both the occurrence and the rarity, which is the basis for the VERY_RARE band.

evidence.snippet: The first patient presented at the 4 years of age with recurrent hypoglycemic seizures.
evidence.explanation: A reported child in whom recurrent hypoglycemic seizures were the presenting problem, showing the rare event can still be the entry point.

steps/17.description: Seizures during a severe hypoglycemic episode. Explicitly described as rare, but they have been the presenting event in reported children, so the low frequency does not make them clinically unimportant.

evidence.snippet: Glucose and other sugars taken up by the liver in GSD0 are shunted into the glycolytic pathway leading to postprandial hyperlactatemia and hyperlipidemia
evidence.explanation: Names hyperlipidemia as a downstream consequence of the glycolytic shunt, alongside the lactate rise.

steps/18.description: Reported together with the postprandial lactate rise as a consequence of diverted hepatic carbon flux, rather than as an independent lipid disorder.

evidence.snippet: Glycogen synthase deficiency (glycogen storage disease 0 - GSD 0) caused by mutations in the GYS2 gene is characterized by a lack of glycogen synthesis in the liver.
evidence.explanation: States the edge itself: the GYS2 lesion is what produces absent hepatic glycogen synthesis.

edges/1.description: Loss of the elongating enzyme blocks the glycogen biosynthetic pathway in hepatocytes.

evidence.snippet: In contrast to all other types of glycogenoses, which are characterized by increased glycogen storage, deficiency of glycogen synthase causes a marked decrease in liver glycogen content.
evidence.explanation: Directly evidences this edge - the enzyme deficiency causing decreased, not increased, liver glycogen.

edges/2.description: With synthesis blocked and degradation intact, hepatocyte glycogen content falls below normal instead of accumulating.

evidence.snippet: Postprandial hyperglycemia and hyperlactatemia develop due to the conversion of meal-derived carbohydrates to lactate, as glucose cannot be converted to glycogen.
evidence.explanation: States the causal step explicitly: because glycogen synthesis is unavailable, meal-derived carbohydrate goes to lactate.

edges/3.description: Dietary glucose taken up by the liver cannot be routed to glycogen, so it enters the glycolytic pathway instead.

evidence.snippet: It is a glycogenosis with lack of liver glycogen synthesis, therefore hepatomegaly is not observed in patients with glycogen synthase deficiency.
evidence.explanation: States the causal link from absent synthesis to absent hepatomegaly, which is exactly this edge.

edges/4.description: There is no stored material to expand the hepatocyte mass, so the liver stays a normal size.

edges/5.description: A subnormal reserve cannot sustain glycogenolytic glucose output through a fast.

evidence.snippet: Glycogen storage disease type 0 (GSD-0) is a rare form of fasting hypoglycemia presenting in infancy or early childhood and accompanied by high blood ketones and low alanine and lactate concentrations.
evidence.explanation: Names the full fasting signature this edge produces, including the low lactate that separates it from GSD I.

edges/6.description: Once gluconeogenesis alone can no longer meet glucose demand, blood glucose falls while ketones - the alternative fuel - rise.

edges/7.description: The fasted trough of the daily swing.

edges/8.description: Sustained hyperketonemia and free fatty acid elevation feed back on substrate supply.

edges/9.description: The clinical manifestation of the fasted state.

edges/10.description: Ketone bodies produced in excess spill into the urine.

edges/11.description: Neuroglycopenia during a severe episode can provoke a seizure; this is an uncommon rather than a typical outcome.

evidence.explanation: States the causal step from the synthetic block to the postprandial glucose rise.

edges/12.description: The liver's failure to clear a glucose load into glycogen raises blood glucose, and the diverted flux raises blood lactate.

edges/13.description: Diverted carbon also feeds lipogenesis, giving the hyperlipidemia reported alongside the postprandial lactate rise.

edges/14.description: The fed peak of the daily swing.

edges/15.description: Postprandial glucose exceeding the renal threshold appears in the urine.

edges/16.description: The clinical manifestation of the fed state.

edges/17.description: The lactate arm of the same fed-state abnormality.

edges/18.description: Glucose above the renal threshold appears in the urine.

evidence.snippet: In conclusion, the results demonstrate that GSD-0 is caused by different mutations in the GYS2 gene.
evidence.explanation: The gene-discovery study's own conclusion, establishing GYS2 as the causal gene through linkage plus mutation screening in nine affected children.

evidence.snippet: Expression of the mutated enzymes in COS7 cells indicated severely impaired GS activity.
evidence.explanation: Functional confirmation in a heterologous expression system that the identified alleles are loss-of-function, separate from the genetic association itself.

evidence.snippet: Hepatic glycogen synthase is encoded by GYS2 (MIM 138571) located on 12p12.2 and contains 16 exons spanning over 30 kb of genomic DNA.
evidence.explanation: Gene structure and locus for the hepatic isoform specifically.

evidence.snippet: The current results expand the spectrum of known mutations in GYS2 and suggest that phenotypes of GSD 0 are more variable and less specific than the reported ones.
evidence.explanation: A caveat worth curating alongside the allelic spectrum: the phenotype attached to a GYS2 genotype is less specific than the early case reports implied, so genotype does not predict presentation.

evidence.snippet: Clinical management is therefore based on frequent meals composed of high protein intake during the day and addition of uncooked cornstarch in the evening.
evidence.explanation: States the regimen and its day/night structure, which mirrors the diurnal structure of the disease.

evidence.snippet: Daytime hypoglycemia tends to be mild and frequent snacks, given every 2-4 hours, usually prevents hypoglycemia.
evidence.explanation: Specifies the daytime snack interval that complements the bedtime cornstarch dose.

treatments/0.description: The mainstay, and entirely dietary. Frequent daytime meals high in protein supply gluconeogenic precursors, which works here precisely because gluconeogenesis is intact - the same logic as in GSD VI, and the opposite of GSD I where the gluconeogenic step is itself blocked. Uncooked cornstarch at bedtime, dosed at roughly 1-1.5 g/kg and repeated six-hourly during illness, provides slow-release glucose across the overnight fast. Preventing hyperketonemia is not just symptom relief: it lifts the feedback inhibition of alanine release from muscle, so the diet also protects the gluconeogenic substrate supply it depends on.

evidence.snippet: Since gluconeogenesis is intact, protein supplementation provides gluconeogenic precursors that can be used for endogenous glucose production.
evidence.explanation: States the mechanism claimed on this link, and the reason it works in this disease specifically: the pathway the protein feeds is preserved.

evidence.snippet: In young children, hypoglycemia may still occur on a high protein diet, and uncooked cornstarch (1-1.5 grams/kg) administered at bedtime, and every 6 hours during illness, prevents morning hypoglycemia and ketosis.
evidence.explanation: Gives the cornstarch dose and schedule and the outcome it achieves on this node - prevention of morning hypoglycemia and ketosis.

treatments/0/targets/0.description: Supplies exogenous slow-release glucose and gluconeogenic substrate, bypassing the absent glycogen reserve rather than restoring it.

evidence.snippet: In turn, there is also less dependence upon fatty acid oxidation, and accumulation of free fatty acids and ketones is prevented.
evidence.explanation: Evidences the specific action claimed on this link - the diet suppresses the free fatty acid and ketone accumulation that drives the loop.

treatments/0/targets/1.description: Preventing hyperketonemia removes the inhibitory signal on alanine release from skeletal muscle, protecting the gluconeogenic precursor supply.

evidence.snippet: patients are treated with a diet high in protein with complex, low glycemic index carbohydrates
evidence.explanation: States the carbohydrate composition of the prescribed diet.

treatments/1.description: The other half of the diet, and the half that is specific to this disease rather than shared with the hepatic glycogenoses generally. Because ingested glucose is shunted to lactate, a rapidly absorbed carbohydrate load produces postprandial lactic acidosis; complex low-glycemic-index carbohydrate blunts that. The stated therapeutic goal is explicitly two-sided - prevent the fasting hyperketonemia AND the post-prandial lactic acidosis - which is the diurnal swing restated as a treatment target.

evidence.snippet: The goal of treatment is to prevent hypoglycemia and to minimize the systemic acidosis by preventing post-prandial lactic acidosis and fasting hyperketonemia.
evidence.explanation: Names prevention of post-prandial lactic acidosis as an explicit treatment goal, which is the effect claimed on this link.

treatments/1/targets/0.description: Slowing carbohydrate absorption reduces the glucose flux presented to the liver at any moment, limiting how much is diverted into glycolysis.

evidence.snippet: Perinatally, the mother received a high glucose infusion to stabilize blood glucose levels.
evidence.explanation: The peripartum use of the same intervention, in the only multi-pregnancy report of this disease.

evidence.snippet: Careful monitoring during pregnancy and delivery is, however, necessary to minimize the risk of recurrent hypoglycemia for both mother and child.
evidence.explanation: States the surveillance requirement that accompanies the infusion strategy.

treatments/2.description: Whenever enteral intake is interrupted - surgery, labour, intercurrent illness - the dietary strategy is unavailable and intravenous glucose substitutes for it. Reported for elective surgery under total intravenous anaesthesia with glucose-containing fluids, and peripartum in a woman with three pregnancies. The neonate in that report also needed a glucose infusion postnatally, which is a consequence of maternal hyperglycemia rather than of inherited disease in the infant.

evidence.snippet: To reduce the risk of complications attributed to GSD-0, general anesthesia was administered using a total intravenous anesthesia (TIVA) technique with propofol and remifentanil, along with supplemental glucose-containing intravenous fluids.
evidence.explanation: A worked perioperative case in which supplemental intravenous glucose was used for exactly this purpose, with stable intraoperative glycemia.

treatments/2/targets/0.description: Parenteral glucose replaces the hepatic output the disease cannot supply during periods when feeding is not possible.

evidence.snippet: Because of the variable presentation of this disorder and previous dependence on liver biopsy to confirm diagnosis, it is likely that GSD0 is underdiagnosed.
evidence.explanation: States the underdiagnosis claim and names both of its proposed causes.

evidence.snippet: Children with GSD0 may have a mild phenotype and GSD0 may be underdiagnosed due to subclinical or asymptomatic hypoglycemia.
evidence.explanation: Adds a third ascertainment mechanism - the hypoglycemia can be entirely asymptomatic, so nothing prompts testing.

evidence.snippet: No mutations in GYS2 were found in 49 patients.
evidence.explanation: The negative bound: sequencing GYS2 in fifty children with ketotic hypoglycaemia found one positive, so this presentation is not largely unrecognised GSD 0a.

evidence.snippet: GSD0 is relatively rare in patients presenting with ketotic hypoglycaemia and a normal biochemical profile.
evidence.explanation: The authors' own reading of that negative result, which is the appropriate counterweight to the underdiagnosis claims above.

open_questions/0.rationale: Every quantitative statement about how common this disease is comes from counting papers, and multiple independent sources argue that the count is an undercount rather than a prevalence. The proposed mechanisms of ascertainment failure are specific and testable: the diagnosis historically required a liver biopsy; the fasted presentation is indistinguishable from idiopathic ketotic hypoglycemia, which is common in childhood; the fed presentation is mistaken for early diabetes; and there is no hepatomegaly to prompt the glycogen-storage workup in the first place. Against that, targeted sequencing gives a concrete negative bound - one of fifty children with ketotic hypoglycemia and an otherwise normal profile carried a GYS2 variant - so the disease is not a large hidden fraction of that presentation either. Both bounds are curated here rather than averaged, because they answer different questions: the case count says how many have been found, the sequencing study says how enriched one plausible screening population is.

evidence.snippet: Short stature and osteopenia are common features, but other long-term complications, common in other types of GSD, have not been reported in GSD0.
evidence.explanation: Both halves of the tension in one sentence: two chronic features are common, and the rest are absent from the literature.

evidence.snippet: All four pregnancies in women with GSD 0 described to date occurred with minor complications and resulted in healthy offspring, which underpins the good prognosis and rather benign character of this rare metabolic disease.
evidence.explanation: The strongest available argument for the benign framing, quoted with its own denominator visible - four pregnancies in total.

open_questions/1.rationale: The disease is repeatedly described as comparatively benign, and the supporting observations are real - fasting tolerance improves with age, four reported pregnancies all produced healthy offspring, and the hepatic and renal complications of the storage-side glycogenoses have not been reported. But "have not been reported" in a literature of fewer than thirty patients, most of them children, is a weak negative. Short stature and osteopenia are already acknowledged as common, and both are the kind of finding that accumulates with duration of poor metabolic control rather than appearing early. The question is whether adult follow-up would leave the benign framing intact or add chronic morbidity to it.

evidence.snippet: Immunohistochemistry of hepatic tissue and immunoblotting of a cadmium-stimulated Epstein-Barr virus-transformed lymphoblastoid cell line (LCL) revealed complete absence of HO-1 production.
evidence.explanation: Demonstrates complete absence of HO-1 protein in the index patient, even under cadmium stimulation that normally induces the enzyme. Tagged HUMAN_CLINICAL for the hepatic-tissue immunohistochemistry half of the sentence, which is a direct observation on patient tissue; note that the lymphoblastoid-cell immunoblot in the same sentence is a cell experiment, and the separate LCL hemin-sensitivity result is curated as IN_VITRO on the free-heme node.

evidence.snippet: Western blot analysis confirmed lack of HMOX1 protein upon oxidant stimulation of the patient cells.
evidence.explanation: Independently confirms in a second patient that oxidant stimulation fails to produce HMOX1 protein. Tagged IN_VITRO, not HUMAN_CLINICAL: the measurement is made on cultured patient-derived cells under oxidant challenge, which is a cell experiment even though the cells came from a named patient in a case report.

evidence.snippet: We then confirmed the defective enzyme activity by documenting bilirubin synthesis in PBMC. Control cells showed the expected >4-fold heme-induced increase of bilirubin from 18.8 & 23.6 to 95.9 & 84.6 pmol/mg protein/60min following heme treatment. In contrast, patient cells showed a marginal increase from 21.9 & 26.1 to 33.1 & 27.0 pmol/mg protein/60min.
evidence.explanation: Cultured patient PBMC showed impaired heme-induced bilirubin synthesis. This functional assay supports reduced heme-catabolic activity independently of the protein-inducibility experiment; it is not a direct purified-G139V peroxidase assay.

evidence.snippet: Of the Gly-139 mutants investigated, only G139A catalyzes the NADPH-cytochrome P450 reductase-dependent oxidation of heme to biliverdin, but most of them exhibit a new H(2)O(2)-dependent guaiacol peroxidation activity.
evidence.explanation: Recombinant-enzyme mutagenesis establishes the potential for Gly139 substitutions to exchange oxygenase for peroxidase activity. Tested substitutions were alanine, leucine, phenylalanine, tryptophan, histidine and aspartate, not valine. This provides biochemical support by analogy for the G139V interpretation, not a direct G139V measurement.

evidence.snippet: The strong constitutive expression of HO-1 G139V with defective normal but gained abnormal peroxidase function was paralleled by increased excretion of peroxidation products in the urine of the patient and, to some degree, in his heterozygous parents and heterozygous brother (Table 2).
evidence.explanation: Human urinary oxidation products support the authors' interpretation of abnormal peroxidase activity indirectly. These downstream products do not specifically measure mutant-enzyme peroxidase catalysis. Cultured-cell bilirubin synthesis and recombinant-enzyme experiments are graded separately.

steps/1.description: Biallelic loss-of-function variants in HMOX1 abolish or impair heme oxygenase 1 function. Reported alleles span whole-exon deletion, frameshift, nonsense and missense classes. The p.G139V allele shows that loss of protein abundance is not required: patient cells retained constitutive HO-1 expression but lacked further hemin induction and showed impaired heme-induced bilirubin synthesis. Acquired abnormal peroxidase activity was inferred from human urinary oxidation products and biochemical studies of other Gly139 substitutions. Loss of inducibility alone does not establish these distinct functional defects.

evidence.snippet: Heme oxygenase (HO)-1 constitutes one of the three isozymes of HO, and catalyzes the degradation of heme into biliverdin, carbon monoxide (CO), and free iron, each of which somehow exert potent anti-oxidative stress and anti-inflammatory functions
evidence.explanation: Establishes the three reaction products whose individual loss defines the three product-deficit arms of this pathograph.

evidence.snippet: Among the three isozymes, HO-1 is the only protein rapidly induced upon stimulation with various oxidative stresses
evidence.explanation: Supports the framing that HMOX1 loss removes an inducible protective response that the constitutive isozymes cannot supply.

evidence.snippet: Therefore, any defect in the function of HO-1 would be expected to lead to uncontrollable inflammation in response to certain exogenous insults, such as infection and hemolysis.
evidence.explanation: Links the loss of inducibility specifically to stress-triggered decompensation rather than continuous baseline disease.

evidence.snippet: Our in vitro and in vivo results provide genetic evidence that up-regulation of Hmox1 serves as an adaptive mechanism to protect cells from oxidative damage during stress.
evidence.explanation: Mouse genetic evidence that the induction of Hmox1, not its basal activity, is the protective mechanism lost in this disease.

steps/2.description:
HO-1 is the stress-inducible heme oxygenase isozyme, and the only one rapidly induced by oxidative stress. Its loss therefore does not merely slow basal heme turnover; it removes the surge capacity that normally meets an oxidative or haemolytic insult. Constitutive HMOX2 cannot substitute because it is not inducible.
(Sources differ on how many isozymes to count: the cited review says three, while the cited 2020 case report says two. The discrepancy is the status of HO-3, now generally regarded as a pseudogene rather than a functional enzyme. Nothing in this entry depends on the count, so no number is asserted here; the quoted evidence below preserves each source's own wording.)
The consequence is a single enzymatic block that simultaneously fails to generate biliverdin and bilirubin, fails to generate carbon monoxide, fails to liberate iron for recycling, and leaves the heme substrate itself uncleared. Each of the four downstream arms below is a distinct consequence of this one block.

evidence.snippet: Serum heme concentration was extremely high, at 490 μM (normal range; <1 μM).
evidence.explanation: Direct measurement of circulating free heme at roughly 500-fold the upper limit of normal, which is the accumulation this node asserts.

evidence.snippet: Hemopexin was undetectable by immunoelectrophoresis, indicating the presence of active hemolysis in vivo.
evidence.explanation: Documents exhaustion of the hemopexin heme-scavenging arm in the index patient.

evidence.snippet: An LCL derived from the patient was extremely sensitive to hemin-induced cell injury.
evidence.explanation: Directly demonstrates that HO-1-deficient patient cells are hypersensitive to heme cytotoxicity, the proximate toxic consequence of heme accumulation.

evidence.snippet: Cultured Hmox1(-/-) embryonic fibroblasts demonstrated high oxygen free radical production when exposed to hemin, hydrogen peroxide, paraquat, or cadmium chloride, and they were hypersensitive to cytotoxicity caused by hemin and hydrogen peroxide.
evidence.explanation: Mouse-derived cells reproduce the same heme hypersensitivity, supporting heme itself as the proximate cytotoxic species.

steps/3.description: Uncleared heme reaches extreme plasma concentrations (490 micromolar in the index case against a normal value below 1 micromolar), and the scavenging system is overwhelmed: hemopexin is undetectable while haptoglobin is paradoxically elevated rather than consumed, and haptoglobin-haemoglobin complex spills into urine. Free heme is directly cytotoxic and pro-oxidant, and patient-derived cells are hypersensitive to it.

evidence.snippet: Two isoforms exist, heme oxygenase-1 (HMOX1) and heme oxygenase-2 (HMOX2), with CO, biliverdin, and bilirubin implicated in important cellular processes, such as inflammation, cell proliferation, apoptosis, and antioxidant defense.
evidence.explanation: Attributes antioxidant defence specifically to the biliverdin and bilirubin products lost in this disease.

evidence.snippet: He has been suffering from persistent hemolytic anemia characterized by marked erythrocyte fragmentation and intravascular hemolysis, with paradoxical increase of serum haptoglobin and low bilirubin.
evidence.explanation: The index case documents the defining paradox of haemolysis with low rather than raised bilirubin.

evidence.snippet: Persistently elevated LDH despite low bilirubin levels led Greil et al. to analyze the HMOX1 gene, revealing the homozygous G139V mutation.
evidence.explanation: Shows the haemolysis-without-bilirubin signature is discriminating enough to have driven a diagnosis.

steps/4.description: Biliverdin, and the bilirubin derived from it by biliverdin reductase, is a physiologically significant antioxidant. Because HO-1 is the sole route to biliverdin under stress, HO-1 deficiency removes this antioxidant sink. The same block explains the disease's most discriminating laboratory paradox: a patient with brisk intravascular haemolysis has LOW serum bilirubin and no jaundice, because the bilirubin normally produced from the liberated heme is inadequately generated. Persistently elevated LDH alongside low bilirubin is the combination that prompted the diagnosis in at least one reported case.

evidence.snippet: CO directly controls the inflammatory state of a given tissue, and at the same time regulates the microcirculation within target organs by acting as a gaseous mediator
evidence.explanation: Establishes the anti-inflammatory and vasoregulatory roles of the CO product that HO-1 deficiency eliminates.

evidence.snippet: We recently demonstrated in in vitro cultures that a CO-releasing molecule, tricarbonyldichlororuthenium (II) dimer suppressed TNF-α-induced up-regulation of tissue factor and plasminogen activator inhibitor type 1 by human umbilical vein endothelial cells.
evidence.explanation: Add-back of CO in vitro reproduces the anticoagulant and anti-inflammatory effect whose absence is proposed to explain the patients' coagulopathy. Support is indirect because this is a pharmacological add-back in cultured cells, not a demonstration in patient tissue. The quote is given in full so that the agent is identifiably a CO donor.

steps/5.description: CO produced by heme ring opening acts as a gaseous mediator that restrains inflammatory signalling and regulates the microcirculation and the coagulation and fibrinolysis balance. Loss of endogenous CO is the arm most often invoked to explain the disproportionate endothelial and coagulation abnormalities of this disease, but this attribution is a hypothesis rather than a demonstrated mechanism in patients: the supporting experiment is an add-back, in which exogenous CO-releasing molecules suppress TNF-alpha-driven upregulation of tissue factor and plasminogen activator inhibitor type 1 in cultured human endothelial cells and suppress LPS-induced TNF-alpha production by mononuclear cells. Endogenous CO deficiency has not been measured in a patient, so both downstream edges are marked indirect.

evidence.snippet: Iron deposition was noted in renal and hepatic tissue.
evidence.explanation: Direct human histological evidence of renal and hepatic iron deposition in the index case.

evidence.snippet: Hmox1-deficient adult mice developed an anemia associated with abnormally low serum iron levels, yet accumulated hepatic and renal iron that contributed to macromolecular oxidative damage, tissue injury, and chronic inflammation.
evidence.explanation: The defining mouse experiment establishing the mechanism by which iron is simultaneously deficient in serum and excessive in tissue. Mouse evidence only; the corresponding human histology is cited separately above.

evidence.snippet: Our results indicate that Hmox1 has an important recycling role by facilitating the release of iron from hepatic and renal cells, and describe a mouse model of human iron metabolic disorders.
evidence.explanation: States the recycling role of Hmox1 whose loss produces the tissue-iron trapping.

steps/6.description: Most body iron is recycled from senescent erythrocytes rather than absorbed from the diet, and HO-1 catalyses the step that liberates that iron. Its loss traps iron inside hepatic parenchymal cells and renal tubular epithelium instead of releasing it for erythropoiesis. The resulting state is counter-intuitive and is a recognised diagnostic trap: heavy tissue iron deposition and marked hyperferritinaemia coexist with normal or low serum iron, and with anaemia that does not respond to iron supplementation.

evidence.snippet: In vivo and in vitro studies have indicated that impaired HO-1 production results in progressive monocyte dysfunction, unregulated macrophage activation and endothelial cell dysfunction, leading to catastrophic systemic inflammatory response syndrome.
evidence.explanation: Names monocyte dysfunction and unregulated macrophage activation as consequences of impaired HO-1, converging on systemic inflammation.

evidence.snippet: They showed progressive death of macrophages in the liver and spleen throughout the process of erythrophagocytosis and the resultant heme release in vivo, causing significant damage to the organs and intense inflammation of the surrounding tissues.
evidence.explanation: Mouse evidence for the specific cellular mechanism, macrophage death during erythrophagocytosis, underlying this node.

evidence.snippet: The cytoplasm of circulating monocytes was vacuolated, and expressions of many monocyte surface antigens were markedly reduced.
evidence.explanation: Direct human cellular evidence of monocyte structural and phenotypic abnormality, so this node does not rest on mouse data alone.

evidence.snippet: Previously, we found that macrophages engaged in recycling of red cells were depleted from the tissues of Hmox1(-/-) mice, which resulted in intravascular hemolysis and severe damage to the endothelial system, kidneys, and other organs.
evidence.explanation: Places macrophage depletion causally upstream of the haemolysis and endothelial/renal injury, which is the position this node occupies in the pathograph.

steps/7.description: HO-1 is normally induced to high levels in monocytes and macrophages, which handle the heme load generated by erythrophagocytosis. Without it these cells progressively fail: monocyte dysfunction and unregulated macrophage activation are documented consequences, and mouse work shows macrophages die during erythrophagocytosis. This arm explains both the macrophage-activation-syndrome and haemophagocytic flares seen clinically and, plausibly, the functional asplenia, which in mouse models arises from progressive fibrotic destruction of the splenic red pulp.

evidence.snippet: An abnormal coagulation/fibrinolysis system, associated with elevated thrombomodulin and von Willebrand factor, indicated the presence of severe, persistent endothelial damage.
evidence.explanation: Direct human biomarker evidence of severe persistent endothelial injury.

evidence.snippet: Electron microscopy of renal glomeruli revealed detachment of endothelium, with subendothelial deposition of an unidentified material.
evidence.explanation: Ultrastructural confirmation of endothelial injury in the renal microvasculature, linking this node to the nephritis phenotype.

evidence.snippet: Human HO-1 deficiency has been observed to involve the endothelial cells more severely, resulting in hemolysis and disseminated intravascular coagulation.
evidence.explanation: Independent confirmation that endothelium is the preferentially affected compartment, causally upstream of haemolysis and coagulopathy.

steps/8.description: Vascular endothelium is the tissue most severely affected in human HO-1 deficiency. Markers of endothelial damage (thrombomodulin, von Willebrand factor) are markedly elevated, and glomerular electron microscopy shows frank detachment of endothelium with subendothelial deposits. The coagulation and fibrinolysis systems are grossly deranged, with extraordinarily elevated thrombin-antithrombin complex and fibrin degradation products, yet platelet counts are paradoxically raised rather than consumed, distinguishing this from ordinary disseminated intravascular coagulation.

evidence.snippet:
HO-1 defect is certainly responsible for the renal tubu-
lar injury and subsequent proteinuria and hematuria
seen in this patient.
evidence.explanation: The primary human report explicitly attributes tubular injury and the urine abnormalities to HO-1 deficiency.

steps/9.description: Loss of HO-1-mediated protection permits renal tubular injury in the setting of heme exposure. Tubular injury coexists with glomerular endothelial damage; their relative contributions may differ between patients.

evidence.snippet: Our patient developed severe NSIP, likely due to oxidant-induced injury
evidence.explanation: The primary report proposes oxidant injury as the cause of the fibrotic interstitial pneumonia; this causal attribution remains provisional.

steps/10.description: Oxidant injury is proposed to cause fibrotic nonspecific interstitial pneumonia in HO-1 deficiency. Inflammatory macrophage changes may also contribute; the specific balance of these processes is not established.

evidence.snippet: Peripheral blood smear showed numerous fragmented erythrocytes, Howell-Jolly bodies and nucleated red blood cells.
evidence.explanation: Morphological documentation of erythrocyte fragmentation in the index case.

evidence.snippet: HMOX1-deficiency is a rare autosomal recessive disorder with hallmark features of direct antibody negative hemolytic anemia with normal bilirubin, hyperinflammation and features similar to macrophage activation syndrome.
evidence.explanation: Confirms the haemolysis is antibody-negative, excluding an autoimmune mechanism.

steps/11.description: Persistent intravascular haemolysis with marked erythrocyte fragmentation is a cardinal feature. The blood film shows fragmented erythrocytes together with Howell-Jolly bodies (reflecting the asplenia) and nucleated red cells, and the direct antiglobulin test is negative, excluding an autoimmune cause. Haemolysis both results from and further feeds the heme burden, since each destroyed erythrocyte releases haemoglobin that cannot be catabolised.

evidence.snippet: The devastating clinical courses experienced by these patients indicate the critical importance of HO-1 in holding back rapidly progressive inflammation and organ dysfunction once an overwhelming inflammatory response is ignited by certain triggers.
evidence.explanation: Directly frames the endpoint as failure to restrain a trigger-initiated inflammatory response.

evidence.snippet: Here, we report a 30-year-old male with AA-type renal amyloidosis due to a chronic inflammatory condition of unknown origin.
evidence.explanation: Documents secondary AA amyloidosis as a long-term consequence of the sustained inflammatory state in a genetically confirmed patient.

steps/12.description: The convergent endpoint. Impaired protective responses (reduced bilirubin antioxidant capacity and CO signaling, uncleared cytotoxic heme, trapped redox-active iron, and failing macrophages) produces an unrestrained systemic inflammatory response. Clinically this appears as recurrent fever and rash, nephritis, hepatomegaly, interstitial lung disease, leukocytosis and thrombocytosis, and haemophagocytic or macrophage-activation flares, and in at least one patient progressed to secondary AA amyloidosis. Onset is typically triggered by an exogenous insult such as infection, and once ignited the course is often rapidly progressive and fatal.

evidence.snippet: Fever, absence of the spleen, hemolytic anemia, hematuria/proteinuria, and the absence of jaundice seem to be the common findings in those cases.
evidence.explanation: A review of the reported case series names haemolytic anaemia as a common finding across cases, supporting the association; no population frequency is inferred.

evidence.snippet: Fever and hemolytic anemia were constant findings.
evidence.explanation: Frequency-specific evidence: across the 9 reported patients haemolytic anaemia was a constant finding. This nine-case literature inventory does not provide a disease-wide population estimate.

steps/13.description: Persistent, direct-antiglobulin-negative haemolytic anaemia with intravascular destruction. A hallmark finding in the historical case literature.

evidence.snippet: He has been suffering from persistent hemolytic anemia characterized by marked erythrocyte fragmentation and intravascular hemolysis, with paradoxical increase of serum haptoglobin and low bilirubin.
evidence.explanation: Documents marked erythrocyte fragmentation in the index patient.

steps/14.description: Numerous schistocytes on the peripheral blood film, reflecting mechanical and oxidative erythrocyte damage on an injured endothelial surface.

evidence.snippet: Repeated measurements of serum bilirubin concentration were always low, at 0.1–0.3 mg/dL.
evidence.explanation: Direct repeated low-bilirubin measurements in the index patient support hypobilirubinaemia; absence of visible jaundice alone would not establish it.

evidence.snippet: More importantly, bilirubin remained low or within normal ranges in all cases, despite the presence of active hemolytic anemia. Paradoxical normo- or hypobilirubinemia in the presence of active hemolytic anemia is certainly the first denominator of HO-1 deficiency.
evidence.explanation: Low or normal bilirubin despite active haemolysis was present in all 9 reported cases. Note the review's own wording is "low or within normal ranges", so frank hypobilirubinaemia — the HP term bound here — is not shown to be universal even though the failure to rise is. That gap is exactly why no `frequency` band is asserted.

evidence.snippet: He has been suffering from persistent hemolytic anemia characterized by marked erythrocyte fragmentation and intravascular hemolysis, with paradoxical increase of serum haptoglobin and low bilirubin.
evidence.explanation: The index case explicitly records low bilirubin coexisting with intravascular haemolysis.

steps/15.description:
The single most discriminating feature. Bilirubin fails to rise despite brisk ongoing haemolysis that would normally produce marked unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia, and jaundice is absent. This is the direct laboratory signature of the enzymatic block, since bilirubin is generated from heme via HO-1.
NOTE on the frequency band, deliberately omitted: the source reports bilirubin as "low or within normal ranges in all cases", which establishes universal failure-to-rise but NOT that frank hypobilirubinaemia (the HP term bound here) occurs in 80% or more of patients. The index case was frankly low at 0.1 to 0.3 mg/dL, but a normal-range value in another patient does not instantiate HP:0033480. Rather than assert a band the evidence does not carry, no `frequency` is given.

evidence.snippet: Further study revealed that serum Hp concentration was extremely elevated (800–1200 mg/dL, normal range; 40–180 mg/dL) and a large amount of Hb-Hp complex was detected in a urine sample from the patient.
evidence.explanation: Direct quantitative measurement of the raised serum haptoglobin this phenotype asserts, roughly 5-fold above the upper limit of normal.

evidence.snippet: These data suggested that the Hb-Hp complex was somehow bypassing the normal scavenger system and overflowing into urine.
evidence.explanation: Offers the proposed explanation for the paradoxical elevation. Support is indirect because the source itself hedges the mechanism as "somehow".

steps/16.description: Haptoglobin is paradoxically elevated rather than consumed, the opposite of what intravascular haemolysis normally produces, because the haptoglobin-haemoglobin complex appears not to be cleared by the normal scavenger route when the downstream catabolic enzyme is absent. The source describes that bypass as happening "somehow", so the mechanism is recorded here as observed rather than established.

evidence.snippet: Increased levels of hepatic enzymes, triglycerides and ferritin were also noted.
evidence.explanation: Records raised ferritin in a genetically confirmed patient.

steps/17.description: Serum ferritin can be markedly elevated during chronic inflammation and macrophage-activation flares. Tissue iron deposition is also reported, but circulating ferritin alone does not quantify iron stores or prove iron overload.
