evidence.snippet: Persistently elevated LDH despite low bilirubin levels led Greil et al. to analyze the HMOX1 gene, revealing the homozygous G139V mutation.
evidence.explanation: Documents persistently elevated LDH and its diagnostic pairing with low bilirubin.

steps/18.description: LDH is extremely elevated during haemolysis and inflammatory tissue injury; the measurement is not specific to either process alone. The combination of high LDH with low bilirubin is the pattern that should prompt HMOX1 testing.

evidence.snippet: We report another case of human HO-1 deficiency in a young girl with congenital asplenia, who presented with severe hemolysis, inflammation, nephritis, which was refractory to therapy with corticosteroids, cyclophosphamide, and rituximab.
evidence.explanation: Documents congenital asplenia in a genetically confirmed patient.

evidence.snippet: Fever, absence of the spleen, hemolytic anemia, hematuria/proteinuria, and the absence of jaundice seem to be the common findings in those cases.
evidence.explanation: Absence of the spleen is listed among findings common to the reported case series. The pooled absence/hypoplasia descriptions do not establish a frequency for anatomic asplenia alone.

steps/19.description: An absent spleen is reported in several patients, sometimes described as congenital. Other patients have a small, infarcted, normal-sized, or enlarged spleen; hypoplasia and functional hyposplenism are not equivalent to anatomic absence.

evidence.snippet: Fever, absence of the spleen, hemolytic anemia, hematuria/proteinuria, and the absence of jaundice seem to be the common findings in those cases.
evidence.explanation: Names haematuria and proteinuria among the findings common to reported cases.

evidence.snippet: Hematuria and proteinuria were observed in all of the Japanese and Indian cases.
evidence.explanation: Quantifies the renal involvement across the Japanese and Indian cases, though the review notes urine findings were not reported for two further patients, so no frequency band is asserted here.

steps/20.description: Renal involvement with haematuria is common and refractory to immunosuppression. Glomerular endothelial detachment on electron microscopy provides the structural correlate.

evidence.snippet: Fever, absence of the spleen, hemolytic anemia, hematuria/proteinuria, and the absence of jaundice seem to be the common findings in those cases.
evidence.explanation: Names proteinuria among findings common to the reported cases.

steps/21.description: Proteinuria accompanies the glomerular endothelial injury; in the rat model proteinuria occurs with focal segmental sclerosis and podocyte changes.

evidence.snippet: Here, we report a 30-year-old male with AA-type renal amyloidosis due to a chronic inflammatory condition of unknown origin.
evidence.explanation: The primary observation of AA-type renal amyloidosis in the patient this phenotype is drawn from, including the age at which it was found.

evidence.snippet: Clinical exome sequencing (CES) confirmed the HMOX-1 deficiency diagnosis related to homozygous missense G139V mutation.
evidence.explanation: Establishes that the patient carrying this phenotype has a molecularly confirmed biallelic HMOX1 genotype, so the amyloidosis is attributable to this disease rather than to an unrelated inflammatory diagnosis.

evidence.snippet: Also, HMOX-1 deficiency-related systemic AA-type amyloidosis has not been reported before.
evidence.explanation: The authors state this was the first such report, which is why the phenotype is curated without a frequency band rather than as a recurring feature.

steps/22.description: Reactive (AA-type) amyloid deposition in the kidney, arising as a late complication of the sustained systemic inflammatory state rather than as a direct consequence of the enzymatic block. Reported in a single genetically confirmed patient — a 30-year-old man homozygous for the p.G139V missense variant, in whom AA-type renal amyloidosis was the presenting problem and the underlying inflammatory condition was of unknown origin until clinical exome sequencing was performed. The authors propose chronic inflammation as the driver of the AA deposits; the timing and frequency of this complication are not established. Reported once, so no frequency band is asserted; see the terminal pathophysiology node "Systemic Inflammatory Response and Progressive Organ Injury" for the causal chain, and the notes block for why amyloidogenesis conformance is deferred rather than declared.

evidence.snippet: Fever and hemolytic anemia were constant findings.
evidence.explanation: Frequency-specific evidence: fever was a constant finding across the 9 historical patients. The small published-case denominator is retained here without a disease-wide frequency band.

steps/23.description: Recurrent febrile inflammatory episodes, often infection-triggered, are frequently the presenting feature and initially suggest a systemic autoinflammatory syndrome or systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis.

evidence.snippet: The patient is a six-year-old boy with severe growth retardation.
evidence.explanation: Documents severe growth retardation in the index patient.

steps/24.description: Growth retardation can be severe but is not universal. In at least one patient growth was normal until inflammatory episodes began and then fell away, suggesting a contribution from chronic illness. The relative contributions of inflammation, nutritional status and prolonged steroid exposure remain uncertain.

evidence.snippet: More importantly, increases in leukocyte and platelet counts were invariably noted in all cases, which is contrary to the phenomenon observed in HLH patients.
evidence.explanation: Frequency-specific evidence: raised leukocyte counts were invariable across the nine historical cases. This is not a population estimate; the contrast with typical HLH-associated cytopenias remains diagnostically useful.

evidence.snippet: Episodes included hemolysis without hyperbilirubinemia, immunodeficiency, hepatomegaly with mild transaminitis, asplenia, leukocytosis, thrombocytosis, joint pain and features of macrophage activation with negative autoimmune serologies.
evidence.explanation: Records leukocytosis among the flare features in a confirmed patient.

steps/25.description: Marked and persistent leukocytosis, part of the chronic inflammatory signature; infection can additionally trigger or amplify flares.

evidence.snippet: Here, we describe a phenotype expansion for HMOX1-deficiency to include not only asplenia and hepatomegaly, but also interstitial lung disease with cholesterol granulomas and inflammatory flares with hemophagocytosis present in the bone marrow.
evidence.explanation: Names hepatomegaly as an established feature of the disorder.

steps/26.description: Hepatomegaly with hepatic iron deposition and mild transaminitis. Liver biopsy may show Kupffer cell siderosis, haemophagocytosis and extramedullary haematopoiesis.

evidence.snippet: Here, we describe a phenotype expansion for HMOX1-deficiency to include not only asplenia and hepatomegaly, but also interstitial lung disease with cholesterol granulomas and inflammatory flares with hemophagocytosis present in the bone marrow.
evidence.explanation: The report that established interstitial lung disease as part of the HMOX1-deficiency phenotype.

evidence.snippet: In this study, we describe a patient with severe interstitial lung disease, frequent episodes of hyperinflammation non-responsive to immunosuppression, and fatal pulmonary hemorrhage.
evidence.explanation: A second, independent genetically confirmed patient with severe interstitial lung disease, establishing the pulmonary phenotype as recurrent rather than a single-case observation, and independently corroborating the failure of immunosuppression curated in the treatments section.

steps/27.description: Nonspecific interstitial pneumonia with pleural fibrosis and cholesterol granulomas, progressing to chronic respiratory failure. This was a phenotype expansion recognised only in 2020 and is a cause of death.

evidence.snippet: Here, we describe a phenotype expansion for HMOX1-deficiency to include not only asplenia and hepatomegaly, but also interstitial lung disease with cholesterol granulomas and inflammatory flares with hemophagocytosis present in the bone marrow.
evidence.explanation: Documents bone-marrow haemophagocytosis during inflammatory flares.

steps/28.description: Haemophagocytosis in bone marrow and liver with features of macrophage activation syndrome. Several patients were initially investigated for familial haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis before HMOX1 was tested, and one achieved sustained remission of HLH signs on the HLH-2004 protocol while inflammatory markers remained elevated.

evidence.snippet: An abnormal coagulation/fibrinolysis system, associated with elevated thrombomodulin and von Willebrand factor, indicated the presence of severe, persistent endothelial damage.
evidence.explanation: Documents the abnormal coagulation and fibrinolysis system in the index patient.

steps/29.description: Grossly abnormal coagulation and fibrinolysis parameters with elevated thrombin-antithrombin complex, fibrin degradation products and D-dimer, and reduced fibrinogen. The index patient initially lacked an apparent bleeding tendency, but later cases include clinically important and fatal bleeding.

evidence.snippet: Hypertension and intracranial hemorrhage are certainly related to the basic pathology of HO-1 deficiency. However, these symptoms were not constantly observed in HO-1 deficiency patients.
evidence.explanation: Attributes hypertension to the disease pathology while explicitly denying that it is constant, which is why this phenotype carries no frequency band.

steps/30.description: Hypertension featured in the terminal deterioration of both the index Japanese case and the first Indian case, and is mechanistically consistent with the endothelial and renal injury. The review is explicit that it is NOT a constant finding, so no frequency band is asserted.

evidence.snippet: Her terminal stage was complicated by hypertension and intracranial hemorrhage, as observed in the initial Japanese case.
evidence.explanation: Documents intracranial haemorrhage in the terminal phase of two independent genetically confirmed patients.

steps/31.description: Intracranial haemorrhage occurred in the terminal phase in both the index Japanese case and the first Indian case, consistent with the combination of endothelial injury and the deranged coagulation and fibrinolysis system. Like hypertension it is attributed to the disease pathology but is not a constant finding, so no frequency band is asserted.

evidence.snippet: On first admission, the patient revealed massive pericardial effusion without any evidence of infectious diseases or malignancies.
evidence.explanation: Documents massive pericardial effusion as the presenting feature in a genetically confirmed patient, with infection and malignancy excluded.

steps/32.description: Massive pericardial effusion was the presenting feature in the Iranian p.K204X patient, who later died with heart failure and ascites. Reported in a small number of patients, including a steroid-responsive effusion during an inflammatory flare in the US case; no frequency band is asserted.

evidence.snippet: Hyperlipidemia was another prominent finding, with triglycerides at 638 mg/dL (normal range; 32-115) and total cholesterol at 552 mg/dL (normal range; 128-219), showing a predominance of low-density lipoprotein cholesterol.
evidence.explanation: The quantitative source for the index-case lipid values and the LDL predominance stated in this phenotype's description.

evidence.snippet: Increased levels of hepatic enzymes, triglycerides and ferritin were also noted.
evidence.explanation: Records raised triglycerides in a second, independent genetically confirmed patient, supporting hyperlipidaemia as a recurring rather than isolated feature.

steps/33.description: Marked hypertriglyceridaemia was present in the index case (638 mg/dL) and recurred in later patients. Chronic inflammation and corticosteroid treatment are possible contributors; a disease-specific mechanism is not established.

evidence.snippet: Levels of hepatic enzymes such as LDH, AST, and ALT uniformly showed significant elevations.
evidence.explanation: Frequency-specific evidence: the review reports AST and ALT elevation in the five Indian cases discussed in that paragraph, not uniformly in all patients. No disease-wide frequency is inferred from that subgroup.

steps/34.description: AST and/or ALT can rise during organ injury. AST is not liver-specific, and the index patient had raised AST with normal ALT. Reported in the Indian case series, the Iranian case and the US case.

evidence.snippet: Hyperlipidemia was another prominent finding, with triglycerides at 638 mg/dL (normal range; 32–115) and total cholesterol at 552 mg/dL (normal range; 128–219), showing a predominance of low-density lipoprotein cholesterol.
evidence.explanation: The measured cholesterol elevation supports this endpoint separately from hypertriglyceridaemia.

steps/35.description: Marked total and LDL cholesterol elevation was documented in the index patient; prolonged corticosteroid exposure is a competing explanation for the lipid abnormality.

evidence.snippet: In 1999, Yachie et al. reported on a 26-month-old boy who had been admitted with recurrent fever, generalized erythematous rash, and joint pain [17].
evidence.explanation: The index case had generalized erythematous rash, without evidence for a more specific papular eruption.

steps/36.description: A generalized erythematous rash accompanied febrile inflammatory illness in the index patient; a papular morphology is not established.

evidence.snippet: The patient had characteristic facial features such as a flat nasal bridge, frontal bossing, and prominent edema of the eyelids.
evidence.explanation: The eyelid location is explicit; neither upper nor lower lids are specified.

steps/37.description: Prominent eyelid edema was reported in the index patient. Its frequency and cause remain uncertain.

evidence.snippet: In 1999, Yachie et al. reported on a 26-month-old boy who had been admitted with recurrent fever, generalized erythematous rash, and joint pain [17].
evidence.explanation: Joint pain was part of the index patient presentation.

evidence.snippet: Bilateral knee arthritis was clinically noted accompanying myalgias and arthralgias with morning stiffness, although subsequent knee x-rays showed no erosions.
evidence.explanation: The US patient had clinically observed arthritis and arthralgias.

steps/38.description: Joint pain occurs during inflammatory illness; knee arthritis with morning stiffness was documented in the US patient.

evidence.snippet: Abdominal CT scan revealed a small poorly perfused spleen which correlated well with the Howell-Jolly bodies and schistocytes on peripheral smear.
evidence.explanation: Imaging establishes a small spleen rather than complete anatomic absence.

steps/39.description: A small, poorly perfused spleen with evidence of infarction was documented in the US patient. This acquired course is distinct from congenital absence of splenic tissue.

evidence.snippet: More importantly, increases in leukocyte and platelet counts were invariably noted in all cases, which is contrary to the phenomenon observed in HLH patients.
evidence.explanation: Frequency-specific evidence: raised platelet counts were invariable across the nine historical cases; subsequent reports include thrombocytopenia. No disease-wide band or invariant distinction from HLH/DIC is asserted.

evidence.snippet: Episodes included hemolysis without hyperbilirubinemia, immunodeficiency, hepatomegaly with mild transaminitis, asplenia, leukocytosis, thrombocytosis, joint pain and features of macrophage activation with negative autoimmune serologies.
evidence.explanation: Records thrombocytosis in a genetically confirmed patient.

steps/40.description: Platelet counts can remain markedly raised despite coagulopathy, with contributions from hyposplenia and inflammatory flares. This pattern is diagnostically useful but not invariant; later cases include thrombocytopenia.

evidence.snippet: Clinical profiles were characteristic, in that he presented with microcytic anemia and progressive hepatosplenomegaly at 3 months old.
evidence.explanation: The p.G139V Turkish patient had splenic enlargement rather than asplenia.

evidence.snippet: Sonography showed mild hepatosplenomegaly with a distorted spleen (Fig. 1 B).
evidence.explanation: The later pulmonary case independently documents splenic enlargement.

steps/41.description: An enlarged spleen is an alternative human presentation; it does not exclude HMOX1 deficiency. Size may regress during the disease course.

evidence.snippet: He was found on thorascopic lung biopsy to have extensive interstitial fibrosis, consistent with the fibrotic nonspecific interstitial pneumonia (NSIP) pattern, in addition to cholesterol granulomas.
evidence.explanation: Biopsy establishes pulmonary fibrosis, beyond an unspecified interstitial lung abnormality.

steps/42.description: Extensive interstitial and alveolar septal fibrosis was demonstrated on lung biopsy in the US patient with fibrotic NSIP.

evidence.snippet: We present a young boy who presented with chronic respiratory failure due to nonspecific interstitial pneumonia following a chronic history of infection-triggered recurrent hyperinflammatory flares.
evidence.explanation: The report explicitly attributes chronic respiratory failure to nonspecific interstitial pneumonia.

steps/43.description: Progressive chronic hypoxic respiratory failure complicated severe fibrotic NSIP and ultimately caused death in the US patient.

evidence.snippet: A 10-year-old boy was admitted for diagnostic lung biopsy in the setting of progressive chronic hypoxic respiratory failure and recurrent hyperinflammatory episodes.
evidence.explanation: The hypoxic respiratory failure supports persistent oxygenation impairment, beyond an isolated viral bronchiolitis episode.

steps/44.description: Hypoxemia occurred with progressive chronic respiratory failure as well as acute respiratory flares.

evidence.snippet: However, he experienced sudden fulminant pulmonary bleeding and expired at the age of five years and eleven months.
evidence.explanation: The primary case narrative documents fatal pulmonary bleeding without a preceding thoracic biopsy complication.

steps/45.description: Spontaneous fulminant pulmonary bleeding was fatal in the later German patient. This is distinct from the post-biopsy hemothorax in the US case.

evidence.snippet: During hospitalization, hepatomegaly was found along with mild transaminitis (AST 301 U/L, ALT 74 U/L), direct antiglobulin test negative hemolytic anemia (hematocrit 24.7%) and hemoglobinuria without microscopic red blood cells.
evidence.explanation: The absence of microscopic red cells distinguishes haemoglobinuria from haematuria.

steps/46.description: Urinary haemoglobin without microscopic erythrocytes was documented during haemolysis in the US patient, distinct from true haematuria.

evidence.snippet: Heme oxygenase-1 (HMOX1) catalyzes the metabolism of heme into carbon monoxide, ferrous iron, and biliverdin.
evidence.explanation: Identifies the reaction HMOX1 catalyses, so absence of the protein directly abolishes that catalytic step.

edges/1.description: Loss of functional HO-1 protein directly removes the catalytic capacity to open the heme ring under stress.

evidence.snippet: The gross appearance of the serum combined with the results of absorption spectrum analysis suggested that heme in the form of OxyHb and MetHb was markedly increased in the patient
evidence.explanation: Measured accumulation of circulating heme species in a patient lacking the catabolic enzyme.

edges/2.description: Heme that cannot be catabolised persists in plasma and tissue rather than being cleared.

evidence.snippet: Through biliverdin reductase, biliverdin becomes bilirubin.
evidence.explanation: Establishes that bilirubin is generated only downstream of the biliverdin that heme oxygenases produce. The HO-1 block reduces this pathway without establishing complete absence of bilirubin synthesis by other isoforms.

edges/3.description: Loss of HO-1 reduces stress-induced biliverdin production and the bilirubin derived from it; retained HO-2 does not restore the inducible response.

evidence.snippet: Heme oxygenases are rate-limiting enzymes that catalyze the degradation of heme to carbon monoxide (CO), ferrous iron, and biliverdin, which then becomes bilirubin via the action of biliverdin reductase.
evidence.explanation: Identifies CO as a direct product of the rate-limiting heme oxygenase step, so loss of HO-1 reduces the stress-inducible contribution to CO production.

edges/4.description: CO is generated stoichiometrically by the ring-opening reaction, so the enzymatic block removes HO-1-derived production without eliminating all endogenous CO sources.

evidence.snippet: Our results indicate that Hmox1 has an important recycling role by facilitating the release of iron from hepatic and renal cells, and describe a mouse model of human iron metabolic disorders.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the causal dependence of hepatic and renal iron release on Hmox1 activity.

edges/5.description: Iron cannot be liberated from heme and released from hepatic and renal cells for reuse.

evidence.snippet:
HO-1 defect is certainly responsible for the renal tubu-
lar injury and subsequent proteinuria and hematuria
seen in this patient.
evidence.explanation: A disease-specific causal interpretation is made in the primary patient report.

edges/6.description: Loss of the inducible HO-1 response permits heme-associated tubular injury.

evidence.snippet: Our patient developed severe NSIP, likely due to oxidant-induced injury
evidence.explanation: The primary report proposes oxidant injury as the cause of the fibrotic interstitial pneumonia; this causal attribution remains provisional.

edges/7.description: Loss of HO-1-mediated oxidant protection is proposed to drive the pulmonary injury.

evidence.snippet: An LCL derived from the patient was extremely sensitive to hemin-induced cell injury.
evidence.explanation: Demonstrates that HO-1-deficient patient cells are killed by heme, which is the cytotoxicity this edge invokes. The edge is indirect because the cells tested were lymphoblastoid, not endothelial, so heme cytotoxicity toward patient endothelium specifically is inferred rather than shown.

edges/8.description: Free heme is cytotoxic and pro-oxidant, and vascular endothelium is the compartment most severely affected in the human disease. The link between the two is inferred rather than directly measured in patient endothelium.

evidence.snippet:
Furthermore, a high LDL choles-
terol level itself, coupled with free heme, may acceler-
ate the oxidative injury of the vascular endothelium
(25). High thrombomodulin concentration indicates
that the patient’s endothelium suffers constant injury
(26, 27). Electron microscopic study of the patient’s
kidney shows peculiar detachment of the endothelium
within the glomeruli. These changes may lead to the
constant destruction of erythrocytes and platelets.
evidence.explanation: The primary authors propose endothelial oxidative injury as an intermediate linking free heme to blood-cell destruction; this is a qualified causal interpretation rather than co-occurrence evidence.

edges/9.description: Free heme can aggravate vascular oxidative injury, which in turn contributes to erythrocyte destruction and fragmentation.

evidence.snippet: A detailed analysis of the first human case of HO-1 deficiency revealed that HO-1 is involved in the protection of multiple tissues and organs from oxidative stress and excessive inflammatory reactions, through the release of multiple molecules with anti-oxidative stress and anti-inflammatory functions.
evidence.explanation: Supports the general route from lost antioxidant products to unrestrained oxidative and inflammatory tissue injury. Support is indirect because the source attributes protection to the products collectively rather than isolating the bilirubin arm.

edges/10.description: Loss of the bilirubin antioxidant sink leaves oxidative stress unbuffered, amplifying inflammatory tissue injury.

evidence.snippet: He has been suffering from persistent hemolytic anemia characterized by marked erythrocyte fragmentation and intravascular hemolysis, with paradoxical increase of serum haptoglobin and low bilirubin.
evidence.explanation: The index patient had low bilirubin despite haemolysis; the enzymatic block explains the failure of bilirubin production to rise appropriately.

edges/11.description: Reduced bilirubin generation can yield frankly low serum bilirubin; some affected patients instead remain within the normal range.

evidence.snippet:
The mechanism of hyperlipidemia, with high choles-
terol and triglyceride levels, is not clear. Prolonged cor-
ticosteroid therapy alone may explain the levels seen in
this patient. Bilirubin is a known antioxidant (20), and
it also acts as a scavenger for degraded LDL cholesterol
(21–24). Impaired bilirubin production in this patient
might also be responsible for the abnormally elevated
serum cholesterol.
evidence.explanation: This is the authors' hypothesis, not an established or exclusive mechanism; the competing steroid explanation is retained.

edges/12.description: Impaired bilirubin production is proposed as one contributor to elevated cholesterol; prolonged corticosteroid treatment is a competing explanation.

evidence.snippet: We recently demonstrated in in vitro cultures that a CO-releasing molecule, tricarbonyldichlororuthenium (II) dimer suppressed TNF-α-induced up-regulation of tissue factor and plasminogen activator inhibitor type 1 by human umbilical vein endothelial cells.
evidence.explanation: CO add-back restrains exactly the endothelial procoagulant programme this edge asserts is unrestrained without CO. Support is indirect because it is a pharmacological add-back in cultured cells rather than a measurement in patients.

edges/13.description: Without endogenous CO, endothelial tissue factor and PAI-1 are not restrained and the coagulation and fibrinolysis balance is lost.

evidence.snippet: CO directly controls the inflammatory state of a given tissue, and at the same time regulates the microcirculation within target organs by acting as a gaseous mediator
evidence.explanation: Attributes direct control of tissue inflammatory state to CO, so its absence removes that control.

edges/14.description: Loss of the CO brake on inflammatory signalling permits an unrestrained systemic inflammatory response.

edges/15.description: Iron that cannot be recycled out of the macrophage accumulates, and serum ferritin rises. The edge is hedged because ferritin is not a clean readout of that: it is also an acute-phase reactant, and this disease produces a sustained systemic inflammatory state that raises it independently of iron. The phenotype's own description, its evidence and its reports_on interpretation all make that point — circulating ferritin does not quantify tissue iron stores here — so this edge should not assert an iron-loading mechanism more confidently than the record it points at. Which of the two contributions dominates in any given patient is not established by anything cited.

evidence.snippet: They showed progressive death of macrophages in the liver and spleen throughout the process of erythrophagocytosis and the resultant heme release in vivo, causing significant damage to the organs and intense inflammation of the surrounding tissues.
evidence.explanation: Ties the heme released during erythrophagocytosis directly to macrophage death in the HO-1-deficient state.

edges/16.description: Iron and heme overload within erythrophagocytosing macrophages impairs and ultimately kills them.

evidence.snippet: Hmox1-deficient adult mice developed an anemia associated with abnormally low serum iron levels, yet accumulated hepatic and renal iron that contributed to macromolecular oxidative damage, tissue injury, and chronic inflammation.
evidence.explanation: States the causal contribution of accumulated tissue iron to oxidative damage, tissue injury and chronic inflammation.

edges/17.description: Deposited redox-active iron drives macromolecular oxidative damage and chronic inflammation in liver and kidney.

edges/18.description: Absent splenic tissue, reported in several patients and sometimes described as congenital. Drawn from the macrophage node because the spleen is the organ of the red-pulp macrophage compartment this disease disables. Note the entry curates four different splenic outcomes — absence, hypoplasia, normal size and enlargement — because all four are reported; none excludes the diagnosis.

edges/19.description: A small, poorly perfused, infarcted spleen — an acquired course distinct from congenital absence, and curated separately for that reason.

edges/20.description: The opposite splenic presentation, which may regress during the disease course. Curated because its presence does not exclude HMOX1 deficiency.

evidence.snippet: In vivo and in vitro studies have indicated that impaired HO-1 production results in progressive monocyte dysfunction, unregulated macrophage activation and endothelial cell dysfunction, leading to catastrophic systemic inflammatory response syndrome.
evidence.explanation: States the causal chain from unregulated macrophage activation to catastrophic systemic inflammatory response syndrome.

edges/21.description: Unregulated macrophage activation drives the haemophagocytic and macrophage-activation-syndrome flares that dominate the clinical course.

evidence.snippet: A bone marrow biopsy demonstrated extensive histiocyte activation with phagocytosis of nucleated red blood cell precursors.
evidence.explanation: Activated histiocytes were directly observed phagocytosing precursors in the patient.

edges/22.description: Unregulated macrophage activation includes phagocytosis of blood-cell precursors during inflammatory flares.

edges/23.description: Bleeding into the brain, the most consequential expression of the endothelial injury and coagulopathy this node describes.

evidence.snippet: Human HO-1 deficiency has been observed to involve the endothelial cells more severely, resulting in hemolysis and disseminated intravascular coagulation.
evidence.explanation: Places endothelial involvement causally upstream of the haemolysis in this disease.

edges/24.description: A damaged endothelial surface shears circulating erythrocytes, producing the fragmentation and schistocytes seen on the blood film.

evidence.snippet: In vivo and in vitro studies have indicated that impaired HO-1 production results in progressive monocyte dysfunction, unregulated macrophage activation and endothelial cell dysfunction, leading to catastrophic systemic inflammatory response syndrome.
evidence.explanation: Names endothelial cell dysfunction among the converging routes to systemic inflammatory response syndrome.

edges/25.description: Endothelial dysfunction propagates vascular inflammation and contributes to nephritis and multiorgan injury.

evidence.snippet: Human HO-1 deficiency has been observed to involve the endothelial cells more severely, resulting in hemolysis and disseminated intravascular coagulation.
evidence.explanation: The clinical report explicitly attributes coagulation abnormalities to endothelial involvement.

edges/26.description: Endothelial injury disrupts coagulation and fibrinolysis.

edges/27.description: Released from lysed erythrocytes; the standard laboratory marker of intravascular haemolysis.

edges/28.description: The paradox of this disease, and worth an edge rather than omission precisely because it runs backwards: intravascular haemolysis normally consumes haptoglobin, but here the haptoglobin-haemoglobin complex is not cleared, because clearing it is the job of the macrophage compartment this disease disables. A normal or high haptoglobin does not exclude the diagnosis.

evidence.snippet: Therefore, any defect in the function of HO-1 would be expected to lead to uncontrollable inflammation in response to certain exogenous insults, such as infection and hemolysis.
evidence.explanation: Names haemolysis specifically as an insult that, without HO-1, leads to uncontrollable inflammation.

edges/29.description: Ongoing haemolysis supplies the inflammatory and oxidative burden that the absent HO-1 response cannot contain.

evidence.snippet: He has been suffering from persistent hemolytic anemia characterized by marked erythrocyte fragmentation and intravascular hemolysis, with paradoxical increase of serum haptoglobin and low bilirubin.
evidence.explanation: The clinical process includes red-cell destruction and fragmentation; these edges expose its corresponding phenotype endpoints.

edges/30.description: Intravascular erythrocyte destruction causes haemolytic anaemia.

evidence.snippet: He has been suffering from persistent hemolytic anemia characterized by marked erythrocyte fragmentation and intravascular hemolysis, with paradoxical increase of serum haptoglobin and low bilirubin.
evidence.explanation: The clinical process includes red-cell destruction and fragmentation; these edges expose its corresponding phenotype endpoints.

edges/31.description: Fragmented erythrocytes are the morphological manifestation of this haemolytic process.

evidence.snippet: During hospitalization, hepatomegaly was found along with mild transaminitis (AST 301 U/L, ALT 74 U/L), direct antiglobulin test negative hemolytic anemia (hematocrit 24.7%) and hemoglobinuria without microscopic red blood cells.
evidence.explanation: The primary patient had haemoglobinuria during intravascular haemolysis, without urinary red cells.

edges/32.description: Intravascular red-cell lysis releases haemoglobin that can enter the urine.

evidence.snippet: The free Hb released during hemolysis scavenges serum nitric oxide leading to vasoconstriction, which results in hypertension.
evidence.explanation: The clinical review proposes this indirect mechanism. It is not a patient-level nitric-oxide measurement or an exclusive explanation for hypertension.

edges/33.description: Scavenging of nitric oxide by free haemoglobin is proposed to contribute to vasoconstriction and hypertension; renal injury may also contribute.

edges/34.description: Hepatic involvement in the systemic inflammatory and iron-deposition process.

edges/35.description: The biochemical correlate of that hepatic injury.

edges/36.description: Raised triglycerides in the systemic inflammatory state.

edges/37.description: Constitutional consequence of chronic systemic inflammation and organ injury.

edges/38.description: Periorbital oedema reported in the inflammatory presentation.

evidence.snippet: Here we report a young man with HMOX1 deficiency that had recurrent autoinflammatory episodes marked by fever, hemolysis and hyperferritinemia with pathologic features similar to MAS and HLH.
evidence.explanation: The febrile episodes are clinical manifestations of the reported autoinflammation.

edges/39.description: Hyperinflammatory flares manifest with recurrent fever.

evidence.snippet: During episodes, his baseline leukocytosis increased from about 20 K/mm3 to exceed 40 K/mm3.
evidence.explanation: The recurrent rise with hyperinflammatory episodes supports reactive leukocytosis; infections may also trigger the flares.

edges/40.description: Inflammatory flares increase circulating leukocyte counts above an already elevated baseline.

evidence.snippet: This inflammatory status could lead to the development of secondary AA-type amyloidosis theoretically. Here, we report a 30-year-old male with AA-type renal amyloidosis due to a chronic inflammatory condition of unknown origin.
evidence.explanation: The genetically confirmed case supports the proposed secondary inflammatory mechanism; the authors frame the disease-specific relation as theoretical.

edges/41.description: Persistent inflammation can lead to secondary AA amyloid deposition in the kidney.

evidence.snippet: He received the Prevnar 13 vaccination and developed another hyperinflammatory episode lasting 4 months complicated by steroid responsive pericardial effusion and presumed inflammatory pneumonitis.
evidence.explanation: The effusion was a steroid-responsive complication of the inflammatory episode, without establishing the same cause in every patient.

edges/42.description: Pericardial effusion can complicate systemic inflammatory flares; steroid responsiveness supports an inflammatory contribution in the US patient.

evidence.snippet: Bilateral knee arthritis was clinically noted accompanying myalgias and arthralgias with morning stiffness, although subsequent knee x-rays showed no erosions.
evidence.explanation: Clinically observed arthritis provides the inflammatory substrate for the reported arthralgias.

edges/43.description: The articular component of systemic inflammation can cause joint pain.

evidence.snippet: The combination of fever, erythematous rash, and joint pain suggested that the patient suffered from a childhood chronic inflammatory illness such as systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis (sJIA) or chronic infantile neurological cutaneous and articular syndrome (alternatively called neonatal-onset multisystem inflammatory disease).
evidence.explanation: The eruption is interpreted as part of the inflammatory presentation; the initial differential diagnoses were subsequently replaced by HMOX1 deficiency.

edges/44.description: The cutaneous component of systemic inflammatory flares can manifest as erythematous rash.

evidence.snippet:
HO-1 defect is certainly responsible for the renal tubu-
lar injury and subsequent proteinuria and hematuria
seen in this patient.
evidence.explanation: The source explicitly places the urine abnormality downstream of renal tubular injury.

edges/45.description: Renal injury produces this urinary manifestation.

evidence.snippet:
HO-1 defect is certainly responsible for the renal tubu-
lar injury and subsequent proteinuria and hematuria
seen in this patient.
evidence.explanation: The source explicitly places the urine abnormality downstream of renal tubular injury.

edges/46.description: Renal injury produces this urinary manifestation.

edges/47.description: Alveolar bleeding, the clinical expression of oxidative injury to the pulmonary vasculature.

evidence.snippet: Our patient developed severe NSIP, likely due to oxidant-induced injury
evidence.explanation: The primary report proposes oxidant injury as the cause of the fibrotic interstitial pneumonia; this causal attribution remains provisional.

edges/48.description: Oxidant injury is proposed to drive the interstitial pneumonitis.

evidence.snippet: He was found on thorascopic lung biopsy to have extensive interstitial fibrosis, consistent with the fibrotic nonspecific interstitial pneumonia (NSIP) pattern, in addition to cholesterol granulomas.
evidence.explanation: The pulmonary process was directly characterized as extensive interstitial fibrosis.

edges/49.description: The documented fibrotic NSIP includes extensive interstitial and alveolar septal fibrosis.

evidence.snippet: We present a young boy who presented with chronic respiratory failure due to nonspecific interstitial pneumonia following a chronic history of infection-triggered recurrent hyperinflammatory flares.
evidence.explanation: The primary report explicitly places chronic respiratory failure downstream of NSIP.

edges/50.description: Severe fibrotic interstitial pneumonia compromises pulmonary function and can progress to chronic respiratory failure.

evidence.snippet: Hyposplenia, initially noted at age 4, was confirmed on serial abdominal imaging, contributed to baseline thrombocytosis, but platelet counts exceeded 1 million frequently during flares, requiring aspirin for coagulation prophylaxis.
evidence.explanation: The authors explicitly attribute baseline thrombocytosis in this patient to hyposplenia.

edges/51.description: Loss of functional splenic tissue contributes to baseline thrombocytosis, with additional rises during inflammatory flares.

evidence.snippet: A 10-year-old boy was admitted for diagnostic lung biopsy in the setting of progressive chronic hypoxic respiratory failure and recurrent hyperinflammatory episodes.
evidence.explanation: The respiratory failure is explicitly hypoxic.

edges/52.description: Failure of pulmonary gas exchange produces hypoxemia.

evidence.snippet: Sequence analysis of the patient's HO-1 gene revealed complete loss of exon-2 of the maternal allele and a two-nucleotide deletion within exon3 of the paternal allele.
evidence.explanation: The founding genotype-phenotype observation establishing HMOX1 as the causative gene, with two distinct loss-of-function alleles in trans.

evidence.snippet: All cases from India (Cases 2-6) displayed an identical homozygous mutation (p.R44X), indicating a founder effect of this particular mutation in that country.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the p.R44X founder allele and explains why the reported case count exceeds the number of independent mutational events.

evidence.snippet: This mutation was a missense mutation and expression of constitutive HO-1 was increased by cells, but HO-1 levels were not enhanced with additional oxidative stress.
evidence.explanation: Cultured patient cells retained constitutive HO-1 expression without further induction by oxidative stress. This supports an inducibility defect; the distinct catalytic and inferred peroxidase defects require the separate evidence below.

evidence.snippet: Clinical exome sequencing (CES) confirmed the HMOX-1 deficiency diagnosis related to homozygous missense G139V mutation.
evidence.explanation: Independent confirmation of the recurrent homozygous G139V missense allele.

evidence.snippet: We then confirmed the defective enzyme activity by documenting bilirubin synthesis in PBMC. Control cells showed the expected >4-fold heme-induced increase of bilirubin from 18.8 & 23.6 to 95.9 & 84.6 pmol/mg protein/60min following heme treatment. In contrast, patient cells showed a marginal increase from 21.9 & 26.1 to 33.1 & 27.0 pmol/mg protein/60min.
evidence.explanation: Cultured patient PBMC showed impaired heme-induced bilirubin synthesis. This functional assay supports reduced heme-catabolic activity independently of the protein-inducibility experiment; it is not a direct purified-G139V peroxidase assay.

evidence.snippet: Of the Gly-139 mutants investigated, only G139A catalyzes the NADPH-cytochrome P450 reductase-dependent oxidation of heme to biliverdin, but most of them exhibit a new H(2)O(2)-dependent guaiacol peroxidation activity.
evidence.explanation: Recombinant-enzyme mutagenesis establishes the potential for Gly139 substitutions to exchange oxygenase for peroxidase activity. Tested substitutions were alanine, leucine, phenylalanine, tryptophan, histidine and aspartate, not valine. This provides biochemical support by analogy for the G139V interpretation, not a direct G139V measurement.

evidence.snippet: The strong constitutive expression of HO-1 G139V with defective normal but gained abnormal peroxidase function was paralleled by increased excretion of peroxidation products in the urine of the patient and, to some degree, in his heterozygous parents and heterozygous brother (Table 2).
evidence.explanation: Human urinary oxidation products support the authors' interpretation of abnormal peroxidase activity indirectly. These downstream products do not specifically measure mutant-enzyme peroxidase catalysis. Cultured-cell bilirubin synthesis and recombinant-enzyme experiments are graded separately.

evidence.snippet: With the broader availability of whole exome sequencing, we searched for other mutations which could plausibly explain the phenotype of the patient.De novohomozygous mutations in the SPON2 and IBTK genes, which bind LPS and regulate B-cell function, respectively, were detected in the patient and were found to be heterozygous in the parents. These mutations may contribute to the phenotype.
evidence.explanation: The authors identify homozygous SPON2 and IBTK variants in the same patient and consider them possible modifiers. Their contribution was not functionally established; this limits exclusive attribution of the distinctive inflammatory presentation to HMOX1.

genes/0.notes: HMOX1 encodes heme oxygenase 1, the stress-inducible isozyme. Reported pathogenic genotypes include compound heterozygosity for maternal exon-2 loss plus a paternal two-nucleotide exon-3 deletion (index case), homozygous nonsense p.R44X (a founder allele accounting for the five early Indian cases), homozygous nonsense p.K204X, homozygous missense p.G139V, and compound heterozygous frameshift plus splice-donor alleles. The p.G139V missense allele retained constitutive HO-1 expression but lacked further hemin induction in cultured patient PBMC. A separate cellular assay demonstrated impaired heme-induced bilirubin synthesis. Abnormal peroxidase activity was inferred from urinary oxidation products and biochemical studies of other Gly139 substitutions, rather than directly measured for recombinant G139V. The original patient also carried homozygous SPON2 and IBTK variants considered possible modifiers, so variant-specific inflammatory features cannot be assigned exclusively to HMOX1.

evidence.snippet: Avoidance of exogenous stress along with appropriate treatment may prevent early death in these patients.
evidence.explanation: Supports stress avoidance plus supportive management as the current practical approach.

treatments/0.description: No disease-modifying therapy exists. Management is supportive, together with the infection precautions appropriate to asplenia. Because decompensation is typically triggered by an exogenous insult, avoidance of oxidative and infective stress is itself part of management.

evidence.snippet: The anemia proved resistant to iron supplementation and the patient was dependent on red cell transfusion.
evidence.explanation: Establishes red cell transfusion dependence and the failure of iron supplementation.

treatments/1.description: Transfusion support for the chronic haemolytic anaemia. Note that iron supplementation is NOT appropriate: the anaemia arises from failure to recycle iron out of tissue stores, not from iron deficiency, and reported patients were resistant to it.

evidence.snippet: We report another case of human HO-1 deficiency in a young girl with congenital asplenia, who presented with severe hemolysis, inflammation, nephritis, which was refractory to therapy with corticosteroids, cyclophosphamide, and rituximab.
evidence.explanation: Documents refractoriness to three separate immunosuppressive agents in a confirmed patient.

evidence.snippet: Therapy with corticosteroid, anti-IL-1R, anti-IL-6, and cyclosporine had been tried but with minimal benefit.
evidence.explanation: Independent confirmation that broad anti-cytokine and immunosuppressive therapy provides minimal benefit.

evidence.snippet: These agents are effective in some cases, but conventional anti-inflammatory/immunosuppressive therapies resulted in therapeutic failure in HO-1 deficiency cases for two reasons.
evidence.explanation: Reports the review's conclusion of inadequate disease control; individual symptomatic responses are documented elsewhere. Quoted as a complete sentence rather than the trailing fragment, so the contrast with other diseases is visible in the quote.

evidence.snippet: He was steroid responsive and therefore treated with oral prednisone 10 mg twice daily.
evidence.explanation: The US patient had symptomatic steroid responsiveness despite later progression; this qualifies the refractory cases rather than refuting them.

treatments/2.description: Responses vary: refractory disease and minimal sustained benefit are common, but corticosteroids can temporarily control inflammatory flares, and HLH-directed therapy produced remission of HLH signs in one patient. These responses do not establish correction of the underlying cytoprotective defect or durable disease control. The agents span several classes, so no single therapeutic_agent is bound.

evidence.snippet: Our findings suggest that BMT or the development of specific cell therapies to repopulate patients' tissues with wild-type or reengineered macrophages represent promising approaches for HMOX1 deficiency treatment in humans.
evidence.explanation: The authors' own translational proposal. Recorded as investigational: the supporting data are entirely murine and no treated human case exists.

evidence.snippet: Indeed, allogenic stem cell transplantation has been suggested as a potential treatment and reported to lead to stabilization and prolonged survival in a single case [18].
evidence.explanation: This 2024 clinical paper summarizes the earlier single human transplant report. It supports limited human experience, not a validated cure rate.

treatments/3.description: Investigational therapy supported by macrophage-replacement rescue in Hmox1-null mice and a reported human allogeneic transplant case with stabilization and prolonged survival. Human evidence is limited to a single reported case; durable efficacy and optimal transplantation protocols are not established. In the mouse experiment, donor-derived Kupffer cells restored heme recycling despite transient marrow engraftment. That mechanistic rescue should not be assumed to describe the human transplant outcome in the same detail.

evidence.snippet: These cells, identified as Kupffer cells with high levels of Hmox1 expression, persisted months after transient engraftment of the donor bone marrow and were responsible for the full restoration of heme-recycling ability in Hmox1(-/-) mice and reversing Hmox1-deficient phenotype.
evidence.explanation: Identifies restored macrophage heme-recycling capacity as the specific mechanism by which the intervention reverses the phenotype.

treatments/3/targets/0.description: Replacing HMOX1-deficient macrophages with wild-type macrophages restores the heme-recycling capacity whose loss defines this node.

evidence.snippet: Treatment with 2-phospho-L-ascorbic acid (AA2P) restored cell viability in both models upon hemin-induced stress, with protection requiring functional SVCT2-mediated uptake.
evidence.explanation: The rescue result behind this lead. Tagged IN_VITRO because it is a cell-model rescue in patient-derived LCLs and HEK293T knockouts, with no patient treated.

evidence.snippet: These findings illuminate ascorbic acid metabolism as a critical node in HO-1 deficiency pathophysiology and suggest ascorbic acid supplementation as a potential therapeutic strategy for this rare disorder.
evidence.explanation: The authors' own framing as a *potential* strategy, which is the grade at which this is curated.

treatments/4.description:
A genuine mechanism-directed therapeutic lead, and PRECLINICAL/IN VITRO only. HMOX1-deficient patient-derived lymphoblastoid cells and HEK293T HMOX1-null cells both show substantially reduced intracellular ascorbate (despite compensatory SVCT2 upregulation), abnormal mitochondrial morphology and raised baseline hydrogen peroxide. 2-phospho-L-ascorbic acid restored viability under hemin stress in both models, dependent on functional SVCT2-mediated uptake, and lowered H2O2 without shifting the GSH/GSSG ratio.
Curated as PROPOSED-grade: no patient has been treated, no clinical outcome is reported, and the effect is demonstrated in cell models only. It is listed because it is the one lead in this literature that targets a measured metabolic deficit in patient cells rather than restoring an enzyme that is absent.

evidence.snippet: The prime target of such therapy is HO-1. Pharmacological induction of cellular HO-1 production, use of CO-releasing molecules, or enhancement of Hb-Hp receptor expression by steroid are examples of these approaches.
evidence.explanation: Records the proposed mechanism-directed strategies. Support is indirect because this is an expert proposal in a review, with no efficacy data in HO-1-deficient patients.

treatments/5.description: Investigational and mechanism-directed rather than established. Because the disease is loss of a cytoprotective response, the rational strategy is to restore its products: pharmacological induction of HO-1, CO-releasing molecules, or enhancement of haptoglobin-haemoglobin receptor expression. No clinical efficacy has been demonstrated in HO-1-deficient patients, and pharmacological HO-1 induction is conceptually futile in null genotypes where there is no enzyme to induce. This is recorded as a proposed direction, not a therapy.

evidence.snippet: Compared with HO-1--targeted mice, the present case seems to more severely involve endothelial cells and the reticuloendothelial system, resulting in intravascular hemolysis, disseminated intravascular coagulation, and amyloidosis with a short survival. This contrasts to the predominant iron metabolic disorders of HO-1--targeted mice with a long survival.
evidence.explanation: The strongest anchor for this discussion, because it is a published first-party mismatch claim rather than an inference drawn across papers: the autopsy authors themselves contrast the human organ-system emphasis (endothelium and reticuloendothelial system, short survival) against the predominantly iron-metabolic, long-survival mouse phenotype.

evidence.snippet: In contrast to human cases or mice models, iron deposition was not increased within the tubular epithelium or hepatic parenchyma of the rat model.
evidence.explanation: The explicit statement of rat-human divergence on the tissue-iron phenotype that makes this a model-fidelity question rather than an evidence gap.

evidence.snippet: Red blood cell lifespan is prolonged in heme oxygenase-1 deficient mice compared with wild-type mice.
evidence.explanation: The sharpest divergence of the three, because it runs in the OPPOSITE direction rather than merely differing in degree: mouse erythrocytes live longer, while human patients have shortened red cell survival with fragmentation and intravascular haemolysis.

evidence.snippet: In contrast to the splenomegaly seen in HO-1-knockout mice reported by Poss and Tonegawa, the spleen in these mice showed initial splenomegaly when young, but progressive atrophy as the mice aged.
evidence.explanation: Documents that the splenic phenotype is strain- and age-dependent in mice, so agreement with human asplenia cannot be assumed.

open_questions/0.rationale: Only about a dozen human patients have ever been reported, so a large share of the mechanism in this entry rests on rodent data, and the rodents disagree with the humans, and with each other, on exactly the features that define the disease clinically. Three divergences are documented, and they differ in kind. (i) ORGAN-SYSTEM EMPHASIS AND SURVIVAL: the first human autopsy states the contrast itself, finding endothelial and reticuloendothelial involvement with intravascular haemolysis, DIC and amyloidosis and short survival, against a predominantly iron-metabolic, long-surviving mouse. (ii) ERYTHROCYTE LIFESPAN RUNS THE WRONG WAY: red cell lifespan is *prolonged* in Hmox1-null mice, while human patients have shortened red cell survival with fragmentation — an opposite-direction finding, not a difference of degree, and the reason no conformance to a haemolysis module should be asserted on mouse evidence. (iii) TISSUE IRON: the Hmox1-null rat does not deposit iron in tubular epithelium or hepatic parenchyma at all. Human patients characteristically have asplenia or functional hyposplenism; the original C57BL/6 Hmox1-null mouse instead develops marked splenomegaly, while a mixed-background null strain shows early splenomegaly evolving into fibrotic atrophy and functional hyposplenism, so the apparent mouse-human agreement depends on strain background rather than on Hmox1 genotype alone. The Hmox1-deficient rat diverges more sharply still: it does not develop the hepatic or renal iron deposition that is cardinal in both human patients and mice. That is not merely a missing measurement but a directly contradictory positive finding in a model that otherwise reproduces haemolysis and renal disease, so the iron arm and the haemolysis and renal arms of the rodent literature have different translational standing and should not be inherited wholesale. Conversely, the arms where rodents and humans do converge (failed iron recycling with low serum iron, hypersensitivity of null cells to heme and oxidant stress, and macrophage death during erythrophagocytosis) are the arms where model evidence can reasonably substitute for the human data that will never exist in quantity.

evidence.snippet: The variability of age of onset and the rapidly progressive clinical course suggests the presence of certain compensatory mechanisms to overcome the absence of HO-1 function.
evidence.explanation: The review's own statement that unidentified compensatory mechanisms must exist, which is precisely the gap recorded here.

open_questions/1.rationale: Age at first recognisable symptom in reported patients ranges from 6 months to 15 years, and several patients carrying the identical homozygous p.R44X allele grew and developed normally for over a decade before deteriorating rapidly and dying within months. Identical genotype with a decade of phenotypic variability implies compensatory mechanisms whose identity, capacity and mode of failure are entirely unknown. This matters practically: it means the disease has a long presymptomatic window in which a diagnosis could in principle be made on the low-bilirubin-with-high-LDH signature, and it means the trigger that exhausts compensation is a candidate intervention point.

evidence.snippet: Why these two cases showed a normal-sized spleen or splenomegaly, respectively, remains unclear.
evidence.explanation: The review explicitly identifies unexplained human splenic variability.

evidence.snippet: Further imaging with CTA abdomen demonstrated absent splenic veins and multiple collaterals to a small left kidney, implying that patient’s spleen had infarcted.
evidence.explanation: The primary case supports an acquired infarction interpretation without proving its upstream vascular mechanism.

evidence.snippet: Pathological examination revealed initial enlargement of the red pulp of the spleen underwent progressive fibrotic changes and eventual atrophy and functional hyposplenism in older mice.
evidence.explanation: This mechanism is demonstrated in mice and is not silently transferred to every human splenic phenotype.

open_questions/2.rationale: Human patients show distinct splenic courses. The US imaging suggests infarction, whereas a mixed-background mouse model develops macrophage loss, red-pulp fibrosis and later atrophy. These observations do not establish that the same process causes congenital human asplenia or human splenomegaly. This is uncertainty in developmental versus acquired causal attribution and model translation, not a claim that splenic injury has no mechanism. The documented hyposplenia-to-thrombocytosis consequence is modeled.

evidence.snippet: His growth had been normal by 3 years of age. However, his growth slowed down significantly after the onset of the inflammatory episodes, being less than the 10th percentile for weight and 20th percentile for height at 8 years.
evidence.explanation: The timing supports a chronic-illness contribution but does not distinguish inflammation, nutrition and treatment effects.

evidence.snippet: The patient had characteristic facial features such as a flat nasal bridge, frontal bossing, and prominent edema of the eyelids.
evidence.explanation: The facial and eyelid findings are documented without a demonstrated causal mechanism.

evidence.snippet: Furthermore, array-based Comparative Genomic Hybridization (array-CGH) analysis revealed a 16p13.11 microduplication of paternal origin, which is known to potentially contribute to congenital heart disease, behavioral disorders, developmental delays, brain abnormalities, and skeletal malformations.
evidence.explanation: A coexisting genomic disorder limits attribution of developmental abnormalities to HMOX1 alone.

open_questions/3.rationale: Growth can slow after inflammatory onset, but nutritional state, chronic organ disease and steroid treatment have not been separated. The 2024 pulmonary patient also carries a 16p13.11 duplication that confounds developmental findings. The sources document frontal prominence, a depressed nasal bridge and eyelid edema without establishing a shared morphogenetic cause or identifying renal versus inflammatory fluid accumulation. These unresolved causal attributions are kept distinct from the supported inflammatory and renal paths.

evidence.snippet:
The mechanism of hyperlipidemia, with high choles-
terol and triglyceride levels, is not clear. Prolonged cor-
ticosteroid therapy alone may explain the levels seen in
this patient. Bilirubin is a known antioxidant (20), and
it also acts as a scavenger for degraded LDL cholesterol
(21–24). Impaired bilirubin production in this patient
might also be responsible for the abnormally elevated
serum cholesterol.
evidence.explanation: The primary authors explicitly describe competing lipid explanations.

evidence.snippet: Further study revealed that serum Hp concentration was extremely elevated (800–1200 mg/dL, normal range; 40–180 mg/dL) and a large amount of Hb-Hp complex was detected in a urine sample from the patient.
evidence.explanation: These observations establish the unusual concentrations and handling, not a unique mechanism for the serum elevation.

open_questions/4.rationale: The primary report explicitly leaves hyperlipidaemia unresolved and proposes both corticosteroid exposure and impaired bilirubin production. The latter is retained as a qualified cholesterol edge, not rejected merely because intermediates are unknown. No comparably specific triglyceride mechanism is established. High serum haptoglobin and urinary Hb-Hp complexes document abnormal handling, but the relative roles of altered production and clearance in the high serum concentration have not been resolved.

evidence.snippet: Hypertension and intracranial hemorrhage are certainly related to the basic pathology of HO-1 deficiency. However, these symptoms were not constantly observed in HO-1 deficiency patients.
evidence.explanation: The review recognizes the association but does not isolate the causal route to each hemorrhage.

evidence.snippet: However, he experienced sudden fulminant pulmonary bleeding and expired at the age of five years and eleven months.
evidence.explanation: The fatal complication is reported without a lesion-specific causal demonstration.

evidence.snippet: Hepatomegaly was another characteristic finding and the liver biopsy revealed mild sinusoidal fibrosis, mild microvesicular steatosis, and increased iron deposit within Kupffer cells.
evidence.explanation: Multiple hepatic lesions coexist, without establishing which drives enlargement.

open_questions/5.rationale: The reviewed cases establish hepatic iron deposition, inflammatory injury and, in some patients, amyloid, but do not distinguish their contributions to liver enlargement. Endothelial damage and coagulopathy provide plausible routes to intracranial or pulmonary bleeding; the reports do not attribute each hemorrhage to one of those processes rather than hypertension, pulmonary parenchymal injury or their combination. Supported endothelial-to-coagulopathy and pulmonary injury paths are represented; the unresolved issue is attribution of these particular clinical endpoints, not the absence of modeled intermediates.

evidence.snippet: In gain-of-function SLC40A1 mutations, ferroportin is resistant to hepcidin activity. This leads to unregulated iron export from enterocytes and macrophages and thus, systemic iron overload.
evidence.explanation: States the hepcidin-resistance mechanism, the two cell types the export occurs from, and its systemic consequence.

evidence.snippet: The gain-of-function mutation of ferroportin (SLC40A1) is considered a haemochromatosis type, whereas the loss-of-function mutation of ferroportin (referred to as Ferroportin Disease) is not.
evidence.explanation: Establishes that it is the gain-of-function class, not the loss-of-function class, that belongs on the hemochromatosis pathway modeled here.

evidence.snippet: Gain-of-function variants in the SLC40A1 gene affect the hepcidin binding site on ferroportin.
evidence.explanation: Locates the variants at the hepcidin binding site, which is why hepcidin no longer triggers internalization and degradation of the exporter.

evidence.snippet: Phenotypically and biochemically similar to hepcidin-deficient haemochromatosis
evidence.explanation: Source for this node's claim that the resulting picture resembles the hepcidin-deficient types.

steps/7.description: Gain-of-function SLC40A1 variants sit at the hepcidin binding site on ferroportin, so the exporter is no longer internalized and degraded when hepcidin rises. Iron export from enterocytes and macrophages therefore continues unregulated, and the resulting overload looks like the hepcidin-deficient types even though hepcidin itself is not deficient. This is the mechanism of the type 4 subtype's gain-of-function allelic class.

evidence.snippet: a mutated IRE probe had a higher binding affinity to IRP than did the wild-type probe
evidence.explanation: Gel-shift and Scatchard analysis of the mutant element establishes the tighter IRP binding that keeps H-subunit translation repressed.

evidence.snippet: suppression of H-subunit synthesis and of the increment of radiolabeled iron uptake were observed
evidence.explanation: Overexpression of the mutant subunit in COS-1 cells measured the fall in H-subunit synthesis and in iron uptake that this node records.

evidence.snippet: These data suggest that the A49U mutation in the IRE of H-subunit is responsible for tissue iron deposition and is a novel cause of hereditary iron overload, most likely related to impairment of the ferroxidase activity generated by H subunit.
evidence.explanation: The authors' own attribution of the tissue iron deposition to impaired H-subunit ferroxidase activity.

steps/8.description: The A49U point mutation in the iron-responsive element of ferritin H-subunit mRNA increases the binding affinity of iron regulatory protein for that element, so translational repression of the H subunit is not relieved when iron is plentiful. H-subunit synthesis and iron uptake into ferritin fall, and the reported family's tissue iron deposition is attributed to loss of the ferroxidase activity the H subunit supplies. This is the mechanism of the type 5 subtype.

evidence.snippet: Hereditary hemochromatosis is an inherited iron overload disorder caused by inappropriately low hepcidin secretion leading to increased duodenal absorption of dietary iron, most commonly in C282Y homozygous individuals.
evidence.explanation: Impaired HFE signaling results in low hepcidin in C282Y homozygotes.

steps/9.description: Pathogenic HFE variants (most commonly C282Y homozygosity) blunt hepcidin induction, leaving circulating hepcidin inappropriately low relative to body iron stores.

hypotheses/0.description: Hereditary hemochromatosis (HH), most commonly HFE-related (C282Y homozygotes), arises from inappropriately low hepatic hepcidin expression relative to body iron stores. Hepcidin is the master regulator of systemic iron homeostasis, binding ferroportin on enterocytes and macrophages and causing its internalization and degradation, thereby restricting duodenal iron absorption and reticuloendothelial iron release. Loss-of-function variants in HFE, HJV, TfR2, and HAMP all converge on a final common pathway of relative hepcidin deficiency, leading to chronic increased duodenal iron absorption, transferrin saturation, and progressive non-transferrin-bound iron accumulation in hepatocytes, cardiomyocytes, pancreatic β-cells, and endocrine tissues. Tissue iron toxicity produces cirrhosis, hepatocellular carcinoma, cardiomyopathy, diabetes, hypogonadism, and arthropathy. Therapeutic phlebotomy and investigational hepcidin agonists / ferroportin inhibitors all corroborate the hepcidin-deficient-iron-overload axis as the canonical pathogenic mechanism.

steps/1.description: Hypoxia downregulates the amiloride-sensitive epithelial sodium channel and Na+/K+-ATPase-driven transepithelial sodium transport that normally drives water out of the airspace. Reduced clearance does not by itself cause HAPE but determines how much fluid accumulates once the barrier has failed, and it is the rationale for beta-agonist prophylaxis. Its contribution is secondary to the hemodynamic lesion: in the tadalafil and dexamethasone prophylaxis trial, both drugs prevented HAPE while producing no measurable change in nasal potential difference, the surrogate for alveolar sodium transport.

evidence.snippet: The pulmonary transcapillary escape of radiolabeled transferrin increased slightly from low to high altitude in the HAPE-susceptible subjects but remained within the limits of normal and did not differ significantly from the control subjects.
evidence.explanation: Normal transcapillary protein escape at a stage when capillary pressure is already elevated is the key negative result placing barrier failure downstream of pressure, not as a primary defect.

steps/2.description: Mechanical overload of the alveolar-capillary membrane disrupts the endothelial and epithelial layers and their shared basement membrane — stress failure in West's sense, a physical rupture rather than a signalled junctional opening, although junctional loss accompanies it. The barrier stops excluding protein and erythrocytes, which is why HAPE lavage fluid is high-protein and often blood-tinged. This is the node at which HAPE joins the shared blood-gas barrier pathway, and where a hypoxia-driven disease and a toxicant- or pathogen-driven one become mechanistically the same lesion.

evidence.snippet: Exaggerated pulmonary-artery pressure due to hypoxic vasoconstriction is considered an important pathogenetic factor in high-altitude pulmonary edema.
evidence.explanation: States the exaggerated hypoxic vasoconstriction this node describes as an accepted pathogenetic factor.

steps/3.description: Hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction is normally a matching reflex that diverts perfusion away from poorly ventilated lung. In HAPE-susceptible individuals the response is both excessive in magnitude and regionally heterogeneous. Reduced nitric oxide bioavailability and increased endothelin-1 shift the vasomotor balance toward constriction. The heterogeneity is the pathogenically important feature: it is what converts a global rise in pulmonary vascular resistance into focal capillary overperfusion rather than an evenly shared pressure load.

evidence.snippet: HAPE is initially caused by an increase in pulmonary capillary pressure.
evidence.explanation: The study's own conclusion that capillary hypertension is the initiating hemodynamic lesion.

steps/4.description: Pulmonary capillary pressure rises well above normal. In the Capanna Regina Margherita study, every susceptible subject who went on to develop HAPE had a measured capillary pressure above 19 mmHg while every susceptible subject who did not remained below it — a separation clean enough to make capillary pressure the proximate determinant rather than a correlate. This is a precapillary, not a postcapillary, hypertension: left atrial pressure is normal, which is what makes the resulting edema non-cardiogenic.

evidence.snippet: CONCLUSIONS: Elevated IL-2, IL-10, and TNF in HAPE patients underscore immune dysregulation as a disease driver.
evidence.explanation: Establishes measurable immune dysregulation in HAPE patients; the authors' framing as a driver is their interpretation of a cross-sectional comparison.

steps/5.description: Once the barrier has failed, plasma proteins, cell-free DNA, and debris in the airspace recruit neutrophils and raise circulating cytokines. This amplifies injury and impairs resolution, but it is a consequence of the mechanical lesion, not its cause — the distinction that separates HAPE from ARDS and explains why anti-inflammatory prophylaxis is not the mainstay. Dexamethasone is the partial exception, and its prophylactic benefit tracks with pulmonary artery pressure reduction rather than with an anti-inflammatory effect.

evidence.snippet: Exposure to hypobaric hypoxia, especially when associated with exercise, is a condition potentially leading to the development of the so-called high-altitude pulmonary edema (HAPE).
evidence.explanation: Identifies hypobaric hypoxia, aggravated by exercise, as the initiating exposure.

steps/6.description: Rapid ascent lowers barometric pressure and therefore inspired oxygen tension, producing sustained alveolar hypoxia. Exercise during ascent aggravates it by raising cardiac output and pulmonary blood flow through an already hypoxic vascular bed. This is the environmental trigger; no host lesion is required.

evidence.snippet: A model is also presented to characterize HAPE nonsusceptible versus susceptible individuals based on the efficiency of alveolar-capillary oxygen uptake and estimated morphology of the air-blood barrier.
evidence.explanation: Frames the clinical outcome in terms of alveolar-capillary oxygen uptake efficiency, the gas-exchange endpoint this node describes.

steps/7.description: Protein-rich, often erythrocyte-containing fluid fills the interstitium and alveoli in a characteristically patchy distribution that mirrors the uneven perfusion that produced it. Flooded alveoli are perfused but not ventilated, creating shunt, and the resulting hypoxemia deepens alveolar hypoxia and so intensifies hypoxic vasoconstriction — a positive feedback loop that accounts for the rapid clinical deterioration and for why descent or oxygen, which break the loop at its origin, are so effective.

evidence.snippet: High-altitude pulmonary edema (HAPE) is caused by exaggerated hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction associated with decreased bioavailability of nitric oxide in the lungs and by impaired reabsorption of alveolar fluid.

edges/0.description: Alveolar hypoxia is the direct stimulus for hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction; in susceptible individuals the response is disproportionate.

edges/1.description: Uneven precapillary constriction concentrates the cardiac output in the unconstricted capillary segments, raising pressure there rather than distributing it.

genes/2.notes: Deliberately left unbound. PMID:42254115 prints the symbol as "P1B1 cytochrome genes", which is not a valid HGNC symbol, and the primary references behind that sentence were not consulted. An earlier draft of this entry expanded it to CYP1B1 and bound hgnc:2597; that binding was withdrawn because a PubMed check returns no papers linking CYP1B1 to high altitude pulmonary edema, while CYP11B2 (aldosterone synthase) returns several and CYP17A1 one. The most likely reading is therefore CYP11B2, but reading "P1B1" as "11B2" is an inference this citation does not license, and substituting one guess for another would be no better than the first. treatments/0.description: Immediate descent is the definitive treatment and reverses the disease by removing the hypoxic stimulus. Where descent is impossible, supplemental oxygen, and portable hyperbaric therapy where available, substitute for it. Both act at the top of the causal chain rather than on the edema itself.

treatments/0/targets/0.description: Raising inspired oxygen tension abolishes the hypoxic stimulus for pulmonary vasoconstriction and breaks the hypoxemia feedback loop.

evidence.snippet: RESULTS: HAPE resolution in the CPAP plus high FiO2 group and the high flow oxygen alone group was similar.
evidence.explanation: The trial found no advantage of adding CPAP to high-flow oxygen; PARTIAL records an effective but not additive intervention.

treatments/1.description: CPAP added to high-flow oxygen was tested in a randomized trial against sham CPAP with high-flow oxygen. It did not accelerate resolution beyond oxygen alone, so it is not an established addition where oxygen is available; the trial is recorded here because the negative result is the clinically useful finding.

treatments/1/targets/0.description: Positive airway pressure recruits flooded alveoli and reduces shunt, acting on the gas-exchange consequence rather than the vascular cause.

evidence.snippet: Seven of the 11 subjects who received placebo but only 1 of the 10 subjects who received nifedipine had pulmonary edema at 4559 m (P = 0.01).
evidence.explanation: A randomized placebo-controlled result directly demonstrating prophylactic efficacy.

treatments/2.description: A dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker that lowers pulmonary artery pressure. In susceptible mountaineers ascending rapidly to 4,559 m it cut HAPE incidence from 7 of 11 on placebo to 1 of 10. It remains the standard pharmacologic prophylaxis for individuals with a HAPE history.

treatments/2/targets/0.description: Calcium channel blockade relaxes pulmonary arterial smooth muscle, lowering the pressure that drives capillary stress failure.

evidence.snippet: High-altitude pulmonary edema developed in 7 of 9 participants receiving placebo and 1 of the remaining 8 participants receiving tadalafil but in none of the 10 participants receiving dexamethasone (P = 0.007 for tadalafil vs. placebo; P < 0.001 for dexamethasone vs. placebo).
evidence.explanation: Randomized evidence of prophylactic efficacy for both tadalafil and dexamethasone.

treatments/3.description: A phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitor that potentiates nitric-oxide-mediated pulmonary vasodilation, addressing the reduced nitric oxide bioavailability that underlies exaggerated hypoxic vasoconstriction. An alternative to nifedipine in susceptible individuals.

treatments/3/targets/0.description: PDE5 inhibition raises cGMP in pulmonary vascular smooth muscle, opposing hypoxic vasoconstriction.

evidence.snippet: CONCLUSIONS: Both dexamethasone and tadalafil decrease systolic pulmonary artery pressure and may reduce the incidence of HAPE in adults with a history of HAPE.
evidence.explanation: The trial's conclusion ties the prophylactic benefit to a reduction in systolic pulmonary artery pressure, the proposed mechanism.

treatments/4.description: A glucocorticoid that prevented HAPE outright in the same randomized trial and also lowered systolic pulmonary artery pressure. Notably its benefit tracked with the hemodynamic effect and not with any measurable change in alveolar sodium transport, which is part of why the pressure mechanism is considered primary.

treatments/4/targets/0.description: Reduces the rise in systolic pulmonary artery pressure on ascent.

evidence.snippet: CONCLUSION: Furosemide helps alleviate pulmonary edema in HAPE patients, but further research is needed to clarify its impact on prognosis.
evidence.explanation: A retrospective cohort supporting radiographic benefit while explicitly leaving prognosis unresolved; PARTIAL reflects the authors' own hedge.
